# Coração Delta: 20 years, 20 stories

> Happiness will not be found in a shopping mall.

**Catarina Barreiros**

## 1. A heart called Delta

It all began with a glass heart. Small in size, but immense in meaning. On 28 March 2002, a group of Delta employees decided to surprise Rui Nabeiro on his 71st birthday with a special gift: a red heart, made of glass, which symbolised the wish to turn small acts of volunteering into a true solidarity project. This is how the project Um Coração Chamado Delta was born – an initial trial of what would later become the Associação Coração Delta.

The plan was simple: collect clothes, school supplies, and other essential goods, sort everything after working hours, and, at weekends, deliver it to those who needed it most. Delta sales staff, who travelled the country from north to south, gave crucial support by carrying donations back and forth. In a short time, the group grew and the idea gained scale.

Three years later, on 31 January 2005, what began as a voluntary initiative became official with the creation of the association Coração Delta. With four main areas of action – education, health, solidarity, and social innovation – the mission grew and the impact became deeper. Two years later, in 2007, the Centro Educativo Alice Nabeiro (CEAN) was founded, a space that transformed education in Campo Maior and beyond.

That first glass heart still exists. It is in a display case at CEAN, as a reminder that major changes often begin with small gestures. And, 20 years later, the Coração Delta still beats strongly.

## 2. Lessons for life

From the very beginning, coordination of Coração Delta, as an association, was taken on by Dionísia Gomes who, with two decades of experience in the social field, saw in this project a completely different challenge. “It was a 180-degree turn in my life. I left a very traditional context to build something innovative,” she recalls. Rui Nabeiro, on the other hand, had professional experience in many areas, but not yet in the social field. “I thought he would have a lot to learn in those early days. But I was wrong.” The businessman and entrepreneur proved to be wise, intuitive, and thoughtful. “He led by example. And he always had a positive response for everyone who approached him,” recalls Dionísia, who worked alongside him for 17 years. “Mr. Rui had a wisdom that was not only acquired professionally: it came from his life story and his personality. That taught me more than I can put into words.”

## 3. School is also home

No student is the same as another, and schools must have room to include everyone. This is the purpose of EPIS – Empresários Pela Inclusão Social, an initiative that supports young people in their school journey, helping them overcome emotional and academic difficulties. Through personalised guidance, the programme develops skills such as emotional management, motivation, and improved school performance.

Patrícia Poejo, now 23 years old and a cultural animator at the museums of Campo Maior, joined EPIS in the 7th grade at the Campo Maior Secondary School. “The psychologist Mafalda Minas helped me manage my emotions better. My father was ill at the time, and it was hard to cope with everything. My grades dropped and she helped me recover,” she recalls.

The impact was even greater in the 9th grade, when she lost her father. “It was a very difficult period and Mafalda was always there. She taught me breathing techniques, helped me manage anxiety, and helped me leave that dark place,” recalls Patrícia. The support included one-on-one sessions, memory games, and strategic activities to improve mood and concentration. “When that support came to an end, I missed it a lot. It was a very important experience for me.”

## 4. Generating ideas to change the world

Imagine that someone discovered the wheel but told no one about it. It would not make sense, would it? In this context, CEAN launched the manual Ter Ideias para Mudar o Mundo, created from the desire to share with the world the results of its practice and to bring entrepreneurship to other schools in an innovative way.

One of the main driving forces behind this project was Professor Nuno Brito, then vice-president of Instituto Politécnico de Viana do Castelo. “There was a competition to foster entrepreneurship in polytechnics,” he recalls. “But we quickly realised that a more global method was needed.” Brito then decided to travel the 400 kilometres to Campo Maior – where the Escola Cultural methodology (which promotes transversal, dynamic and empirical training) was already stimulating children’s critical and creative thinking – and extend the invitation to produce this book.

The innovative methodology was synthesized in this manual, created to allow the model to be replicated, including the training of trainers. Reaching teachers meant reaching children, but also parents and communities. Set out in 93 pages, the methodology served as the basis for training sessions and meetings led by the teacher. The manual Ter Ideias para Mudar o Mundo was implemented for five consecutive school years in all schools in the Alto Minho region, reaching children from three to 12 years old.

The results were – and remain – immeasurable. “The value of empowerment is impossible to quantify. But the truth is that we developed the entrepreneurial capacity of the children, not only in a business sense, but also in a social and personal sense. The teachers told us that curiosity about entrepreneurship increased exponentially and that the children were truly empowered. The challenge was met.”

## 5. Alice Nabeiro doubled

From 2007 onwards, Alice Nabeiro was no longer only the name of the matriarch of the Nabeiro family, wife of Rui Nabeiro, but also became the name of the new educational centre – one of Coração Delta’s major commitments in the field of education.

The day the Centro Educativo Alice Nabeiro (CEAN) opened its doors stayed in everyone’s memory. For several reasons, but one in particular: the surprise linked to the choice of the name. The event took place on the very day when Rui Nabeiro turned 76, on 28 March. “The inauguration was special,” recalls Helena Nabeiro, a board member of Coração Delta and daughter of Mrs. Alice. “My mother did not know that the space was going to have her name; it was a surprise. She thought all that bustle had to do with my father, because of his birthday. Usually everything was about Mr. Rui, and so we let her keep that idea while we prepared the surprise.”

Only when the façade was uncovered did Alice Nabeiro discover the surprise. “My mother was not expecting it. She was delighted. But it made perfect sense, because she has been here from the very first minute,” says Helena Nabeiro, who also explains that it was her mother who chose the materials and followed the construction work. João Manuel Nabeiro adds: “The need to create a space where the educational process would begin in the very first years of children’s lives came from both my father and my mother, perhaps even more from my mother, and it has been reflected in the educational centre from the start.”

Over these 17 years, Mrs. Alice has been a regular presence at CEAN. “She used to come in the afternoon and give support. The children knew her well and she loved being with them, playing games, giving them affection,” recalls Helena Nabeiro. “Just mentioning the children makes her eyes light up.”

## 6. Is the sky really the limit?

How does a nine-year-old child from Campo Maior find himself speaking to an audience of hundreds of people about the origin of the Big Bang? The answer is linked to Coração Delta and, in particular, to the Centro Educativo Alice Nabeiro.

Rodrigo Raimundo has always been fascinated by the unknown. Science was his great passion, and CEAN helped to nurture that curiosity. Between the ages of five and twelve, Rodrigo attended the centre’s ATL, where he gained access to new projects, materials, and experiments. “They broadened our horizons, because the town is small compared with the rest of the world,” Rodrigo explains. When he was in the fourth year of school, he was invited to present his own theory on the origin of the Big Bang at TEDx Kids – at the Museu da Eletricidade in Lisbon – where he was the youngest speaker. Two years later, he crossed the border to enter a robotics competition.

For three days, in Badajoz, he competed with a robot programmed as a team, at CEAN, created to complete a course as fast as possible. The group achieved the best time and won the first prize: 150 euros. Instead of keeping the money, they handed it to Rui Nabeiro, asking that it be donated to a social solidarity institution in the region. Now 19 years old, Rodrigo studies Physical Engineering and remains interested in exploring the unknown. It was, however, at CEAN that he learned one of the most important lessons: curiosity takes us far, but it takes us further when accompanied by a sense of community.

## 7. The earlier, the better

“My mother’s heart told me that there was something different,” recalls Patrícia Santos. Lourenço was two years old when his mother realised that something in his development was not progressing as expected. That was when Lourenço began to be supported by Intervenção Precoce do Coração Delta. The service is for children up to six years old who have developmental difficulties, ensuring close and personalised support in Campo Maior, Monforte and Arronches. The work of the specialised team, in collaboration with families, makes a decisive difference in the children’s growth. “I feel that, as a mother, I am part of this multidisciplinary team,” says Patrícia.

In four years, Lourenço made up the year and a half delay in his development. The boy who “did not communicate or maintain eye contact” became a curious, affectionate, and communicative child. “Thanks to Ester, Célia, and Marina,” his mother stresses. “I feel a deep sense of gratitude. I will never be able to tell Lourenço’s story without mentioning their names.”

## 8. Time to Give

Campo Maior, as an inland and border town of the Alentejo, struggles with an ageing and isolated population. In 2010, after a series of news reports describing cases of loneliness among older people, Rui Nabeiro created an initiative that could make a difference. “It was at that time that Dionísia [Gomes] and I presented the project to Mr. Rui who, being very sensitive to these issues, supported us immediately,” recalls Cláudia Gama, coordinator of Tempo para Dar.

The project began in 2010 with volunteers recruited within Grupo Nabeiro during visits to its various departments. “A network of people was created who visited older residents, kept them company, and offered some support,” recalls Cláudia. The project grew, and so did the type of support: in addition to home visits, there were now internal initiatives, such as the sewing workshop, the revival of regional songs, and the flower workshop, where paper flowers – inspired by those of the Festas do Povo de Campo Maior – are made by hand.

At the event celebrating 20 years of Coração Delta, the women who attend the workshop presented Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa with a picture they had made, with paper rosebuds symbolising the dedication and impact of Tempo para Dar.

## 9. Flower Workshop

“It is my second home,” says 78‑year‑old Isabel Estríbio, referring to Tempo para Dar. Created to combat the loneliness of older people, the project offers company, activities, and the chance to learn something new every day. Isabel worked all her life. After raising her ten siblings, she spent 30 years at Novadelta and, later, worked for over a decade in the home of Rui and Alice Nabeiro. “I helped raise the kids in the family,” she says with affection. At 70, she retired for good, but she had too much life in her to stay at home. “When I wanted to join Oficina da Flor, from Tempo para Dar, I was lucky: that very day I stayed there,” she recalls. She made that place a second home and that team of 20 older women a second family.

The group’s daily activities are guided by two monitors, Tânia and Maria João. “They are princesses, they take care of all of us equally, they are special people,” she states. Over these seven years, Isabel has devoted herself to embroidery and to making paper flowers. “I did not know how to make a single flower or a twist, I did not even know how to embroider. I did not have a life for that: I only had time to work, nothing else. But now that I have learned, I know how to do it and I like it very much.” Between conversations, needles, and paper petals, the days pass with joy. “To stop is to die,” she says with determination. “Look, I am even younger now!”

## 10. Coração Delta Tennis Academy

In the name of this project, “Coração Delta” comes before “Academia de Ténis”. This is not by chance. “It is because of Rui Nabeiro, who always said that the heart comes first,” explains Sancho Moura, the mathematics and science teacher at CEAN and a tennis enthusiast. He was the one who presented this idea to the Comendador and gave it shape, in 2017. “Mr. Rui loved the idea straight away,” he recalls.

The launch of the academy had two essential ingredients: the support of the Junta de Freguesia Nossa Senhora da Expetação, which provided the fields, and the enthusiasm of the CEAN students. Eight years later, it has around 40 athletes between 10 and 18 years old, 50 preschool children, and some adults as well. “We bring many people together around this sport,” sums up Sancho.

Training sessions take place from Monday to Friday, in the late afternoon. At weekends, coaches Sancho Moura and Luís Orelhas accompany the athletes to tournaments.

At Coração Delta Academia de Ténis, tennis is seen as more than a sport. “The mental side is essential. We are always making mistakes and surpassing ourselves, and that is how we improve,” the coach explains. Team spirit and a family atmosphere are hallmarks of the club. “Training sessions fly by, and at the end the kids ask: ‘Already?’ – that makes me very happy. I feel that we help create a moment of focus and joy in these children’s daily routine.”

In 2025, the first edition of the Torneio de Ténis Comendador Rui Nabeiro will take place, a federated event that pays tribute to the club’s patron and to the values he always upheld: self‑improvement, resilience, and civic spirit. In the future, the academy aims to continue growing and to inspire more young people to discover tennis as a way of life.

## 11. Campo Maior European Solidarity Town

Campo Maior Vila Solidária da Europa is a program that, since 2013, has supported unemployed people, vulnerable families, children, and older adults. It works with European funds and acts locally, through local social development contracts. How? By promoting opportunities and building bridges between workers and local companies, contributing to the development of social and civic skills, and fostering equality and the inclusion of vulnerable people in the community.

Maria Manuel Valentim, the project coordinator, has already lost count of the projects that have most marked her during this period. She highlights, however, the youth volunteering in local institutions during the summer school holidays, which has been repeated for 12 years. “We once had more than 100 volunteers per year,” she says, proud. “It is a way for them to leave home and be called to work on empathy, responsibility, and a sense of community. At the end, they receive a certificate of acquired skills.”

Among the inspiring stories is that of Xavier, a young man passionate about information technology who, at just 15 years old, volunteered at the Comissão Unitária de Reformados Pensionistas e Idosos de Campo Maior, where he dedicated himself to teaching older people how to use social networks, email, and video calls so they could contact family members living far away. The impact was enormous: “At the end of the placement, the older people asked a lot about Xavier. They were very fond of him. And he was as well, because he understood the difference he had made in those people’s lives.”

## 12. Girl Move

Alexandra Machado had an established career in the corporate world, including ten years as managing director of Nike Portugal, when she decided to change course. In 2012, inspired by the impact of the Girl Effect Foundation, she realised she wanted to dedicate her experience to social transformation. This is how Girl Move Academy was born, an association that focuses on female education and leadership as tools for the development of Mozambique.

A Girl Move believes that educating a woman transforms a community. “Our mission is to promote a new generation of women who are agents of the country’s development,” concludes Alexandra. At the academy, the innovative model of intergenerational mentoring and learning connects girls with women who can inspire them in different fields, creating a network of social impact. Since its foundation, the project has already changed the lives of more than 15,000 young people, promoting a multiplier effect that reaches entire families.

The project has received international recognition and is supported by several organizations, including Coração Delta. Some of these young women have completed internships in companies of Grupo Nabeiro. This proves that training and empowering women can challenge barriers and create opportunities.

## 13. Pro-Move-Te

The three-in-one of words in the name reflects the spirit of this initiative: dynamic, personalised, fast. Pro-Move-Te is a youth employability programme created in 2017, which brings together nine municipalities in the district of Portalegre and Delta Cafés as partners. David Ferreira, from Campo Maior, took part in the first edition and keeps excellent memories of the three months of training. “I had just moved from Lisbon. I signed up because I wanted to understand which companies existed in the region and what kinds of vacancies there were.” The experience exceeded expectations.

With a dynamic programme, Pro-Move-Te promotes the exchange of experiences and creates opportunities for companies and young unemployed people. How? Through mentoring, coaching and training on CV redesign and improvement of oral communication, as well as organising company visits and promoting direct contact with recruiters.

“I had 10 years of experience in legal services and I ended up finding, through Pro-Move-Te, an opening precisely in that area, at Delta.” David got the job and kept it for six years, then moved internally to the information systems department, where he now works as a help desk technician. “Looking back, Pro-Move-Te was my turning point.”

## 14. 3D Printing Centre for Health

Technology at the service of those who need it most creates miracles. One example is the 3D Printing Centre for Health – an association founded in 2022 by professors and researchers from the research centres LIBPhys and UNIDEMI, in collaboration with FCT Fablab – which develops medical devices through 3D printing with the characteristics required for each case, and offers them free of charge to those who need them most. “We develop devices that are increasingly personalized, so that people gain autonomy and quality of life,” explains Cláudia Quaresma, president of the association.

In less than two years, the 3D Printing Centre for Health has already produced 82 devices for 79 patients and nine healthcare services, including anatomical models that help surgeons prepare for complex operations. Among many remarkable stories, one stands out: a girl who was born without one of her hands. At the age of 8, Carolina received three prostheses made exclusively for her: one for general activities, another to help her eat, and a third so that she could ride a bicycle. The first thing she did, when she tried on the general-activity prosthesis, was to form a heart with her hands.

“The team really had to make an effort not to shed a tear. It was clear that this was very symbolic for Carolina and for her parents.”

With more than 60 volunteers and partnerships with public and private hospitals, the 3D Printing Centre for Health continues to grow with the support of Coração Delta, responding to an increasing number of requests and, in the process, changing lives through innovation and solidarity.

## 15. Café that opens doors

An immersive experience in the world of coffee that combines technical knowledge, personal development, and proximity to the job market. This is Coffee Training, an initiative by Coração Delta aimed at students and young people looking for work. The program takes place at the Centro de Ciência do Café, in a day dedicated to learning and networking. Dragos Cristian Florea, 22 years old, an industrial maintenance technician at Delta, took part in Coffee Training in 2020 while attending a postgraduate course in Metalomecânica and Metalurgia. “We went as a group of 15 students. We visited the Centro de Ciência do Café, learned the entire history of coffee, and carried out some interpersonal exercises,” he recalls. For Cristian, the experience was excellent. “That day helped us prepare for the job market.” Contact with the world of coffee proved particularly useful when he became a locksmith at Delta. “The knowledge I gained was an asset, as were the contacts I made,” he says.

## 16. LIVING ROOM

Without bureaucracy or half-answers, ESTAR is committed to being present where its help is most needed. Founded in 2019 by Madalena Palma and Inês Féria, the association provides an immediate response to social emergencies, supporting associations and communities in critical moments, such as fires, floods, or other types of emergencies. “We realised that the speed of the response was innovative and distinctive,” recalls Madalena Palma.

During the pandemic, ESTAR’s work was particularly significant. Many foreign communities – with precarious jobs and working in sectors that froze from one day to the next – were left without income and, at times, without anything to eat for days. “The van donated by Coração Delta saved us,” Madalena states. It had arrived the previous year and made all the difference.

“We filled the van and delivered food to those who needed it most. I feel we reached many people at the right moment.”

With a food-goods warehouse always ready to respond to crises and a growing support network, currently with 40 volunteers and seven employees, ESTAR operates in the district of Beja and works with other associations from the north to the south of the country.

## 17. CM Factory

A factory of the future could only be connected to young people. CM Factory is the Coração Delta program that challenges the people of Campo Maior to become agents of change in their own town. Through talks, workshops, and round tables, it promotes debate on entrepreneurship, innovation, and the retention of talent in the most depopulated regions.

Sara Henriques, a physiotherapist from Campo Maior, took part in one of the initiatives as a member of GEDA – Grupo de Ecologia e Desportos de Aventura, an association that energises the town with several types of activities, the best known of which is the Festival dos Grous.

“It was interesting to sit down and talk about Campo Maior and the possibilities that the town still has to explore,” he explains. They discussed decentralisation, what can be done to encourage young people to settle in the interior of the country, and how to energise the territory. “These are issues that affect us deeply. From that day, what remained above all was the sense that we are not alone in this.”

## 18. Catholic Mission in Guinea-Bissau

The Catholic Mission in Guinea-Bissau is not a formal association, but rather an organized group of volunteers that, since 2021, has been providing essential support to local communities. João Mendes is the spokesperson for this group and one of its most active volunteers. Twice a year he travels to the field on mission, accompanied by electricians, teachers, and doctors, ensuring that the most urgent needs are met.

The impact is already visible on several fronts. The group began by creating a nursery for 80 babies and then a primary school for 57 children, where one of the classrooms received a symbolic name: Sala Delta.

“It is a joint effort. Without the more than 80 volunteers and without the support of organisations such as Coração Delta, it would be impossible,” he states. A second nursery for 97 children was also added, in the locality of Suzana.

It was precisely in that place, on the northern border of Guinea-Bissau with Senegal, that the last mission took place, at the end of 2024. A total of 830 people benefited directly, a record that left the volunteers very satisfied. “With just one donation from Coração Delta of solar panels and batteries, we managed to light up the village of Suzana. Today, there is power in the school, the health post, and the local radio station.” The impacts are sometimes difficult to measure, but they are felt. “The gratitude of those people for the simplest things we can imagine is immense. For me, this project is an awakening,” says João Mendes.

## 19. Entrepreneurial Talent

Spending weekends in parent meetings is not exactly most people’s idea of a dream plan, let us admit it. But “it was transformative,” says Jorge Grifo, recalling the initiative promoted by the Casa Interior project, from Coração Delta, in 2018. The challenge was to discuss, together with other parents connected to the Centro Educativo Alice Nabeiro, talent in children – how to discover it, encourage it, and help it grow.

There were three months of group sessions, which included conversations and practical activities. What was learned proved so useful that it resulted in a “manual made with love”, as Jorge describes it. Talento Empreendedor: Dicas para pais e mães is a guide that aims to help parents rethink how they support their children’s growth and how they value the signs that reveal their talents. The book brings together what Jorge – and the other participants in the sessions – discovered about parenthood and what inspired them so deeply.

“I have a 14-year-old boy and an 11-year-old girl. The work we did led me to think about our daily life and how, even in the middle of all our tasks, we need to find time to talk with calm and presence. It is through small signs that we understand how they are and who they really are. Sometimes ten minutes of conversation make all the difference. That was the lesson that stayed with me most throughout the entire project.”

## 20. A new heart…

Two decades later, the glass heart offered to Rui Nabeiro once again marked a moment full of meaning. On 31 January 2025, the association celebrated 20 years with a ceremony at the Centro Educativo Alice Nabeiro in Campo Maior. The event brought together several public figures, including the President of the Republic, Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa, and the president of Coração Delta, Rita Nabeiro, in a moment that recognised the social impact of the association over the past two decades.

One of the most symbolic moments was the presentation to the President of a replica of the glass heart that marked the birth of Coração Delta, as a way to highlight the association’s ongoing commitment to social solidarity. But the surprise did not end there. Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa also brought a special gesture: the decoration of Coração Delta as an Honorary Member of the Order of Merit, as a way to recognise its work in social inclusion, education, health, and community support.

It all began with a glass heart. Small in size, but immense in meaning. On 28 March 2002, a group of Delta employees decided to surprise Rui Nabeiro on his 71st birthday with a special gift: a red heart, made of glass, which symbolised the wish to turn small acts of volunteering into a true solidarity project. This is how the project Um Coração Chamado Delta was born – an initial trial of what would later become the Associação Coração Delta.

The plan was simple: collect clothes, school supplies, and other essential goods, sort everything after working hours, and, at weekends, deliver it to those who needed it most. Delta sales staff, who travelled the country from north to south, gave crucial support by carrying donations back and forth. In a short time, the group grew and the idea gained scale.

Three years later, on 31 January 2005, what began as a voluntary initiative became official with the creation of the association Coração Delta. With four main areas of action – education, health, solidarity, and social innovation – the mission grew and the impact became deeper. Two years later, in 2007, the Centro Educativo Alice Nabeiro (CEAN) was founded, a space that transformed education in Campo Maior and beyond.
That first glass heart still exists. It is in a display case at CEAN, as a reminder that major changes often begin with small gestures. And, 20 years later, the Coração Delta still beats strongly.

From the very beginning, coordination of Coração Delta, as an association, was taken on by Dionísia Gomes who, with two decades of experience in the social field, saw in this project a completely different challenge. “It was a 180-degree turn in my life. I left a very traditional context to build something innovative,” she recalls. Rui Nabeiro, on the other hand, had professional experience in many areas, but not yet in the social field. “I thought he would have a lot to learn in those early days. But I was wrong.” The businessman and entrepreneur proved to be wise, intuitive, and thoughtful. “He led by example. And he always had a positive response for everyone who approached him,” recalls Dionísia, who worked alongside him for 17 years. “Mr. Rui had a wisdom that was not only acquired professionally: it came from his life story and his personality. That taught me more than I can put into words.”

No student is the same as another, and schools must have room to include everyone. This is the purpose of EPIS – Empresários Pela Inclusão Social, an initiative that supports young people in their school journey, helping them overcome emotional and academic difficulties. Through personalised guidance, the programme develops skills such as emotional management, motivation, and improved school performance.

Patrícia Poejo, now 23 years old and a cultural animator at the museums of Campo Maior, joined EPIS in the 7th grade at the Campo Maior Secondary School. “The psychologist Mafalda Minas helped me manage my emotions better. My father was ill at the time, and it was hard to cope with everything. My grades dropped and she helped me recover,” she recalls.

The impact was even greater in the 9th grade, when she lost her father. “It was a very difficult period and Mafalda was always there. She taught me breathing techniques, helped me manage anxiety, and helped me leave that dark place,” recalls Patrícia. The support included one-on-one sessions, memory games, and strategic activities to improve mood and concentration. “When that support came to an end, I missed it a lot. It was a very important experience for me.”
4. Generating ideas to change the world

Imagine that someone discovered the wheel but told no one about it. It would not make sense, would it? In this context, CEAN launched the manual Ter Ideias para Mudar o Mundo, created from the desire to share with the world the results of its practice and to bring entrepreneurship to other schools in an innovative way.

One of the main driving forces behind this project was Professor Nuno Brito, then vice-president of Instituto Politécnico de Viana do Castelo. “There was a competition to foster entrepreneurship in polytechnics,” he recalls. “But we quickly realised that a more global method was needed.” Brito then decided to travel the 400 kilometres to Campo Maior – where the Escola Cultural methodology (which promotes transversal, dynamic and empirical training) was already stimulating children’s critical and creative thinking – and extend the invitation to produce this book.

The innovative methodology was synthesized in this manual, created to allow the model to be replicated, including the training of trainers. Reaching teachers meant reaching children, but also parents and communities. Set out in 93 pages, the methodology served as the basis for training sessions and meetings led by the teacher. The manual Ter Ideias para Mudar o Mundo was implemented for five consecutive school years in all schools in the Alto Minho region, reaching children from three to 12 years old.

The results were – and remain – immeasurable. “The value of empowerment is impossible to quantify. But the truth is that we developed the entrepreneurial capacity of the children, not only in a business sense, but also in a social and personal sense. The teachers told us that curiosity about entrepreneurship increased exponentially and that the children were truly empowered. The challenge was met.”

From 2007 onwards, Alice Nabeiro was no longer only the name of the matriarch of the Nabeiro family, wife of Rui Nabeiro, but also became the name of the new educational centre – one of Coração Delta’s major commitments in the field of education.

The day the Centro Educativo Alice Nabeiro (CEAN) opened its doors stayed in everyone’s memory. For several reasons, but one in particular: the surprise linked to the choice of the name. The event took place on the very day when Rui Nabeiro turned 76, on 28 March. “The inauguration was special,” recalls Helena Nabeiro, a board member of Coração Delta and daughter of Mrs. Alice. “My mother did not know that the space was going to have her name; it was a surprise. She thought all that bustle had to do with my father, because of his birthday. Usually everything was about Mr. Rui, and so we let her keep that idea while we prepared the surprise.”

Only when the façade was uncovered did Alice Nabeiro discover the surprise. “My mother was not expecting it. She was delighted. But it made perfect sense, because she has been here from the very first minute,” says Helena Nabeiro, who also explains that it was her mother who chose the materials and followed the construction work. João Manuel Nabeiro adds: “The need to create a space where the educational process would begin in the very first years of children’s lives came from both my father and my mother, perhaps even more from my mother, and it has been reflected in the educational centre from the start.”

Over these 17 years, Mrs. Alice has been a regular presence at CEAN. “She used to come in the afternoon and give support. The children knew her well and she loved being with them, playing games, giving them affection,” recalls Helena Nabeiro. “Just mentioning the children makes her eyes light up.”
6. Is the sky really the limit?

How does a nine-year-old child from Campo Maior find himself speaking to an audience of hundreds of people about the origin of the Big Bang? The answer is linked to Coração Delta and, in particular, to the Centro Educativo Alice Nabeiro.

Rodrigo Raimundo has always been fascinated by the unknown. Science was his great passion, and CEAN helped to nurture that curiosity. Between the ages of five and twelve, Rodrigo attended the centre’s ATL, where he gained access to new projects, materials, and experiments. “They broadened our horizons, because the town is small compared with the rest of the world,” Rodrigo explains. When he was in the fourth year of school, he was invited to present his own theory on the origin of the Big Bang at TEDx Kids – at the Museu da Eletricidade in Lisbon – where he was the youngest speaker. Two years later, he crossed the border to enter a robotics competition.

For three days, in Badajoz, he competed with a robot programmed as a team, at CEAN, created to complete a course as fast as possible. The group achieved the best time and won the first prize: 150 euros. Instead of keeping the money, they handed it to Rui Nabeiro, asking that it be donated to a social solidarity institution in the region. Now 19 years old, Rodrigo studies Physical Engineering and remains interested in exploring the unknown. It was, however, at CEAN that he learned one of the most important lessons: curiosity takes us far, but it takes us further when accompanied by a sense of community.

The three-in-one of words in the name reflects the spirit of this initiative: dynamic, personalised, fast. Pro-Move-Te is a youth employability programme created in 2017, which brings together nine municipalities in the district of Portalegre and Delta Cafés as partners. David Ferreira, from Campo Maior, took part in the first edition and keeps excellent memories of the three months of training. “I had just moved from Lisbon. I signed up because I wanted to understand which companies existed in the region and what kinds of vacancies there were.” The experience exceeded expectations.

With a dynamic programme, Pro-Move-Te promotes the exchange of experiences and creates opportunities for companies and young unemployed people. How? Through mentoring, coaching and training on CV redesign and improvement of oral communication, as well as organising company visits and promoting direct contact with recruiters.

"I had 10 years of experience in legal services and I ended up finding, through Pro-Move-Te, an opening precisely in that area, at Delta." David got the job and kept it for six years, then moved internally to the information systems department, where he now works as a help desk technician. "Looking back, Pro-Move-Te was my turning point."

Technology at the service of those who need it most creates miracles. One example is the 3D Printing Centre for Health – an association founded in 2022 by professors and researchers from the research centres LIBPhys and UNIDEMI, in collaboration with FCT Fablab – which develops medical devices through 3D printing with the characteristics required for each case, and offers them free of charge to those who need them most. “We develop devices that are increasingly personalized, so that people gain autonomy and quality of life,” explains Cláudia Quaresma, president of the association.

In less than two years, the 3D Printing Centre for Health has already produced 82 devices for 79 patients and nine healthcare services, including anatomical models that help surgeons prepare for complex operations. Among many remarkable stories, one stands out: a girl who was born without one of her hands. At the age of 8, Carolina received three prostheses made exclusively for her: one for general activities, another to help her eat, and a third so that she could ride a bicycle. The first thing she did, when she tried on the general-activity prosthesis, was to form a heart with her hands.
“The team really had to make an effort not to shed a tear. It was clear that this was very symbolic for Carolina and for her parents.”

With more than 60 volunteers and partnerships with public and private hospitals, the 3D Printing Centre for Health continues to grow with the support of Coração Delta, responding to an increasing number of requests and, in the process, changing lives through innovation and solidarity.

An immersive experience in the world of coffee that combines technical knowledge, personal development, and proximity to the job market. This is Coffee Training, an initiative by Coração Delta aimed at students and young people looking for work. The program takes place at the Centro de Ciência do Café, in a day dedicated to learning and networking. Dragos Cristian Florea, 22 years old, an industrial maintenance technician at Delta, took part in Coffee Training in 2020 while attending a postgraduate course in Metalomecânica and Metalurgia. “We went as a group of 15 students. We visited the Centro de Ciência do Café, learned the entire history of coffee, and carried out some interpersonal exercises,” he recalls. For Cristian, the experience was excellent. “That day helped us prepare for the job market.” Contact with the world of coffee proved particularly useful when he became a locksmith at Delta. “The knowledge I gained was an asset, as were the contacts I made,” he says.

Without bureaucracy or half-answers, ESTAR is committed to being present where its help is most needed. Founded in 2019 by Madalena Palma and Inês Féria, the association provides an immediate response to social emergencies, supporting associations and communities in critical moments, such as fires, floods, or other types of emergencies. “We realised that the speed of the response was innovative and distinctive,” recalls Madalena Palma.

During the pandemic, ESTAR’s work was particularly significant. Many foreign communities – with precarious jobs and working in sectors that froze from one day to the next – were left without income and, at times, without anything to eat for days. “The van donated by Coração Delta saved us,” Madalena states. It had arrived the previous year and made all the difference.
“We filled the van and delivered food to those who needed it most. I feel we reached many people at the right moment.”

With a food-goods warehouse always ready to respond to crises and a growing support network, currently with 40 volunteers and seven employees, ESTAR operates in the district of Beja and works with other associations from the north to the south of the country.

A factory of the future could only be connected to young people. CM Factory is the Coração Delta program that challenges the people of Campo Maior to become agents of change in their own town. Through talks, workshops, and round tables, it promotes debate on entrepreneurship, innovation, and the retention of talent in the most depopulated regions.

Sara Henriques, a physiotherapist from Campo Maior, took part in one of the initiatives as a member of GEDA – Grupo de Ecologia e Desportos de Aventura, an association that energises the town with several types of activities, the best known of which is the Festival dos Grous.

“It was interesting to sit down and talk about Campo Maior and the possibilities that the town still has to explore,” he explains. They discussed decentralisation, what can be done to encourage young people to settle in the interior of the country, and how to energise the territory. “These are issues that affect us deeply. From that day, what remained above all was the sense that we are not alone in this.”

The Catholic Mission in Guinea-Bissau is not a formal association, but rather an organized group of volunteers that, since 2021, has been providing essential support to local communities. João Mendes is the spokesperson for this group and one of its most active volunteers. Twice a year he travels to the field on mission, accompanied by electricians, teachers, and doctors, ensuring that the most urgent needs are met.

The impact is already visible on several fronts. The group began by creating a nursery for 80 babies and then a primary school for 57 children, where one of the classrooms received a symbolic name: Sala Delta.

"It is a joint effort. Without the more than 80 volunteers and without the support of organisations such as Coração Delta, it would be impossible," he states. A second nursery for 97 children was also added, in the locality of Suzana.

It was precisely in that place, on the northern border of Guinea-Bissau with Senegal, that the last mission took place, at the end of 2024. A total of 830 people benefited directly, a record that left the volunteers very satisfied. “With just one donation from Coração Delta of solar panels and batteries, we managed to light up the village of Suzana. Today, there is power in the school, the health post, and the local radio station.” The impacts are sometimes difficult to measure, but they are felt. “The gratitude of those people for the simplest things we can imagine is immense. For me, this project is an awakening,” says João Mendes.

Spending weekends in parent meetings is not exactly most people’s idea of a dream plan, let us admit it. But “it was transformative,” says Jorge Grifo, recalling the initiative promoted by the Casa Interior project, from Coração Delta, in 2018. The challenge was to discuss, together with other parents connected to the Centro Educativo Alice Nabeiro, talent in children – how to discover it, encourage it, and help it grow.

There were three months of group sessions, which included conversations and practical activities. What was learned proved so useful that it resulted in a “manual made with love”, as Jorge describes it. Talento Empreendedor: Dicas para pais e mães is a guide that aims to help parents rethink how they support their children’s growth and how they value the signs that reveal their talents. The book brings together what Jorge – and the other participants in the sessions – discovered about parenthood and what inspired them so deeply.

“I have a 14-year-old boy and an 11-year-old girl. The work we did led me to think about our daily life and how, even in the middle of all our tasks, we need to find time to talk with calm and presence. It is through small signs that we understand how they are and who they really are. Sometimes ten minutes of conversation make all the difference. That was the lesson that stayed with me most throughout the entire project.”

Two decades later, the glass heart offered to Rui Nabeiro once again marked a moment full of meaning. On 31 January 2025, the association celebrated 20 years with a ceremony at the Centro Educativo Alice Nabeiro in Campo Maior. The event brought together several public figures, including the President of the Republic, Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa, and the president of Coração Delta, Rita Nabeiro, in a moment that recognised the social impact of the association over the past two decades.

One of the most symbolic moments was the presentation to the President of a replica of the glass heart that marked the birth of Coração Delta, as a way to highlight the association’s ongoing commitment to social solidarity. But the surprise did not end there. Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa also brought a special gesture: the decoration of Coração Delta as an Honorary Member of the Order of Merit, as a way to recognise its work in social inclusion, education, health, and community support.

# 177 ways to grind coffee

Did you know that the Centro de Ciência do Café, in Campo Maior, has the largest collection of grinders in the country?

Here you can find them of every kind and shape: Moroccan, Turkish, German, French, Italian, Dutch, electric, manual with a horizontal crank, others with a vertical crank, and even in the D. Maria II style. The collection of coffee grinders at [Centro de Ciência do Café](https://www.centrocienciacafe.com/pt/) already includes 177 pieces from different periods and origins, many of them from the Peugeot brand. The very same one that makes cars. “Because before making cars,” begins museologist Cristina Gameiro, “Peugeot manufactured sewing machines and coffee grinders.”

A significant part of the collection of the Centro de Ciência do Café—which seeks to promote coffee culture and spread knowledge—comes from extensive research carried out by Grupo Nabeiro, through which it was possible to acquire many of the objects on display. “Some, a minority, were donated,” adds Cristina.

The creation of the collection predates the opening of the Centre, in 2014. It even predates the opening of the Museu do Café, inaugurated at the end of 1994, although pieces acquired in more recent years are also part of the collection, which has been built up over time. “When Senhor Comendador began to envision the museum, he did not have only his own holdings and those of Delta Cafés in mind. He also planned to acquire other types of objects and pieces, in order to enrich the space.” Such as, for example, 177 coffee grinders.

In the following pages, we present 12 mills from the collection, each distinct from the others. The remaining 165 are on permanent display at the Centre, which is open to visitors every day from 10:00 to 18:00 (on Saturdays and Sundays only until 14:00).

# The downtown blend

The history of the coffee blend created by Rui Nabeiro is intertwined with that of the Centro de Ciência do Café (CCC).

## What

The exclusive café of the Centro de Ciência do Café

## When

Since 2014

Not because the story is too complex or too complicated to tell, but because these beans – from which a full-bodied, aromatic, pleasant coffee is extracted, easy to drink without sugar – are sold only here, at the Grupo Nabeiro science and technology interpretation and outreach centre, on the Herdade das Argamassas estate, in Campo Maior.

When the team of baristas began working with specialty coffees in 2019, the blend was already present at the CCC. In 2016, the year that marks the opening of the Alquimia shop in the reception area (then only with Delta’s main coffees), it was already being sold in bulk. Since 28 March 2014, when the Centro de Ciência do Café was inaugurated, the blend of the commendatore has been there.

But only later did it become possible to enjoy it on site. “It is a coffee that we make exclusively for visitors to the centre,” says the barista, before mentioning the many customers who come to the shop on purpose to take the blend, which is sold in bulk, as whole beans or freshly ground, or to drink it there.

“It is a different kind of coffee and it is also an experience,” he says. “Our Coffee & Shop is often the first place where people drink a coffee without sugar or without milk. They taste the drink and are pleased with its distinctive flavour, because it is not bitter and it never comes out burnt.” There is a reason for this. Delta baristas receive specific training that allows them to extract the coffee in a way that makes the most of its qualities. And in this blend, a batch whose proportion of arabica and robusta is a secret kept by Rui Nabeiro, quality is something that is never lacking.

Portugal’s 92,212 km2 soon proved too small for the ambition of the founder of Delta. Showing the quality of Delta coffee to the world was Rui Nabeiro’s mission. His dream? To turn the company he founded in a small warehouse in Campo Maior, in 1961, into one of the largest in the world in the coffee business.

Delta’s international expansion happened in two ways: first very slowly, and then suddenly. Only in 1986 did Delta open its first commercial department outside its own facilities – but not far from home, since the choice fell on Badajoz, just a half-hour drive from Campo Maior.

Today, Grupo Nabeiro also has direct operations in France, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Angola, Brazil and China, in addition to Spain. All are commercial operations, with the exception of Angola, where the Group has a manufacturing unit that mainly serves direct consumption, through the Ginga brand, in capsules, beans and ground coffee. There are also another 35 countries, on five continents, where the coffee from Campo Maior arrives through distributors, partners and agents.

In Spain alone there are 330 employees, spread across 16 branches, led by Pedro Cordeiro. “It is our largest operation outside Portugal. We should have a market share of around 4 or 5%, with a stronger presence in Extremadura and Andalusia, where the expansion began. We have been in Spain directly for 37 years, but the connection goes back to the very first day, not least because Delta is located in the Raia area, right next to the border.”

From a global turnover of 460 million euros in 2022, 30% of the business comes from the international area, and, of that share, 40% relates to the Spanish market. “For the economic and financial sustainability of Delta it is important that we are not dependent on the Portuguese market,” admits Rui Miguel Nabeiro. “Twenty years ago, when I joined, Delta was 90% Portugal and, of this, 80% was only the Horeca channel [hotels, restaurants, and cafés]. If we had not made the move to grow in capsules and in the retail market and to grow in international markets, this pandemic period would have been catastrophic. We would have seen 90% of the business disappear, which did not happen.”

The goal now is to grow the Delta Q capsule business and open The Coffee House Experience stores in the land of our Spanish neighbours. “We have four stores in Portugal and we are entering Spain and France. Our aim is to sell a different, high‑quality product, and also to offer experiences built around coffee.”

In 1975, the country was the fourth-largest coffee producer in the world, producing 200,000 tonnes per year. “Angola was once the main source of green coffee for Delta. Mr. Nabeiro went there countless times. That is where it all began,” recalls Alberto Pinto. The most famous trip, the result of a bold move, took place on 10 November 1975, the eve of independence.

“The connection with coffee from Angola is historic and remains in place,” says Alberto Pinto, “which is why Delta sought to return as soon as it could restart the business, which happened 25 years ago.” Rui Miguel Nabeiro explains that this return began with an invitation from the Angolan government.

“My father [João Manuel Nabeiro] went to Angola to visit factories, because they wanted to rebuild the coffee industry. We ended up making a recovery agreement for Liangol, a freeze-dried coffee factory, and we founded Angonabeiro.”

In this way, a factory that had been out of operation since 1984 was rehabilitated and modernised, and in 2001 it began to produce Ginga coffee, an own brand, 100% Angolan, which has as its symbol one of the most emblematic figures in the country’s history. “Ginga coffee was created by us. It is our benchmark brand in Angola, which we also sell in Portugal in capsules and as whole beans,” says Rui Miguel Nabeiro.
But Delta only managed the factory. Only in 2015 did the factory finally pass into the hands of the company from Campo Maior, becoming Delta’s only factory outside Portugal.

Today, Angonabeiro produces Ginga brand coffee in beans, ground, and also in capsules. “These are capsules for the Delta Q system, as is evident,” says Alberto Pinto. While the coffee roasted and packed at the Campo Maior factory is destined for the rest of the world, the coffee from the Angolan factory is mainly for domestic consumption, but not only.

“It has been a profitable business in recent years. It faces one challenge, as Brazil does too, which is the exchange rate. If the currency is favourable, we benefit. If it plunges, the impact shows up immediately in the results,” the CEO says. “It is part of the business.”

The expansion of Delta continues with a focus on countries where the Portuguese emigrant community has a strong presence. And always with direct operations – that is, by opening companies. This is the case of Novadelta France, based in Paris and with branches in Orléans, Lyon, Bordeaux, Pegomas and Nantes. Luxembourg followed, where the local Novadelta was formed in 2011 with the aim of marketing the full range of agri-food products – not only in the Grand Duchy, but also in Belgium and the Netherlands.

After reaching Portuguese communities in Europe, Grupo Nabeiro set course for São Paulo, where it established Delta Foods in 2012. The group had already crossed the Atlantic in 2004, but indirectly, in partnership with another company, Eurobrasil, which placed roasted and packaged coffee from Campo Maior in more than 60 Brazilian coffee shops located mainly in shopping centres, airports, and other high-traffic areas. Eight years later, after direct entries into France and Luxembourg, the group strengthened its presence in Brazil.

“The opportunity arose to sell Delta Q capsules to the Pão de Açúcar group, but the group said it would not buy directly from Portugal, so we had to set up a local company to start the business in Brazil with the Pão de Açúcar group,” recalls Rui Miguel Nabeiro. “Later, the opportunity came up to take a stake in the distributor Q Brasil, which is now the company we have in the state of Espírito Santo [north of Rio de Janeiro].”

From Brazil came the insight that internationalisation could move in two directions. This became clear in April 2023, when the company launched a new coffee shop concept in Portugal. These are stores and kiosks located mainly in shopping centres, airports, and other areas with high pedestrian traffic. If it sounds familiar, that is because it is.

The new concept is called Deltaespresso. It is the network that already has dozens of coffee shops – 75 so far – spread across Brazil. By the end of 2023, the aim is to open six stores and kiosks in Portugal. They will operate under a franchising model, which is a first for Delta. The goal, after importing the concept from Brazil, is to export it. “Deltaespresso has very strong internationalisation potential. We want to reach the global top 10 of coffee brands,” said Rui Miguel Nabeiro at the launch of the concept.

With tea culture in China so dominant, complex, and far‑reaching, with millennia‑old roots that go back to the Han dynasty (206 BC – 220 AD), was it really justified for Delta to open a branch there to sell coffee? Alberto Pinto, director for international markets at Grupo Nabeiro, answers: “China is a country where people drink tea, but it is starting to move into coffee. Delta’s international competitors were entering the market there, so it made sense to establish a presence before coffee consumption took off. It allows us to learn how to work within a very different culture, where consumption habits are very different.”

The connection was already in place. In 2006, Rui Nabeiro and two Portuguese entrepreneurs living in Macau joined forces to open a venue that served Delta coffee and Portuguese pastries, Ruby Café. In Macau, Delta coffee was already sold in some food service spaces, but the brand’s presence in the territory was limited. The aim was to increase exports to China – which had already resumed administration of Macau after centuries of Portuguese rule – but it would still take a few more years to get there.
In China, people drink little coffee, which makes it difficult to distribute it in ground form, as beans, and in Delta Q capsules. For this reason, the business develops mainly through the internet.

Even so, Delta did manage to have a distributor, the result of one of those coincidences in life. “I did a training course in China where I shared a house with a director from PwC. In a conversation I said to him: ‘You, who audit every company here in China, should find us a distributor,’ and they did.” Some retail chains ended up carrying Delta products, while digital channels were explored at the same time. “We ourselves started doing business directly with the Alibaba group. We entered the online stores. It is a business that grows slowly. It is almost entirely digital. In China, everyone buys on the internet.”

After Portugal, Poland is one of the countries where people drink the most Delta Q. In the brand’s international expansion, coffee capsules have played an important role in opening doors in markets where the connection to our country is less evident. That was the case in Poland, where Delta does not have its own commercial department. “We entered in 2019 through an exclusive partnership with Jerónimo Martins. We sell in their stores, in the Biedronka chain, and Delta Q machines are already in 300,000 Polish homes. We have a market share of 22%. It is a source of pride,” says Rui Miguel Nabeiro.

Delta Q coffee is sold in more than 3,300 stores, spread across 1,100 Polish towns and cities. It is a distribution network to be proud of, with Biedronka already the Group Nabeiro’s third-largest customer in terms of turnover. “Things are going as we expected,” says Alberto Pinto. “It is a market with almost 40 million inhabitants, different from what we were used to. There is no Portuguese community of relevant size where we could have started.”
“We compete with our coffee in every format and segment. It is still our main business and it is where we want to be. But we also want to use this structure to sell other products.”

And there are more than 20 categories that Delta sells abroad. This is the case for wine and olive oil from Adega Mayor, olives from the Qampo brand or, to give just one more example, Águas do Alardo.

But the business does not live on its own products alone. Delta also takes on the distribution, abroad, of products from other families. In Switzerland, it partners with Sumol+Compal and distributes Sagres and Super Bock beers. In Angola, it ensures the distribution of Gorila chewing gum and Dan Cake cakes, and it also sells Marimba pasta, one more among the dozens of brands of Grupo Nabeiro. Delta Q remains the product that opens doors, but once inside, Delta goes in with its full offer. “In theory, it is more effective to sell a broad range of products,” explains Alberto Pinto, “although we do not give up on growing our client portfolio.” These are two strategic pillars for growth: internationalisation and diversification.

Dubai represents a remarkable market, where tourism plays an essential role for Delta. “The hotels are very large and we always expect to be able to win an important hotel unit,” says Rui Miguel Nabeiro. “And there are very interesting restaurants that buy our coffee,” he adds. In fact, it is Delta coffee that is served to customers at the Nusr-Et restaurants in Dubai and Abu Dhabi, owned by Turkish chef and entrepreneur Salt Bae – famous on the Internet for his theatrical performance that turned the act of salting meat into a show.

Expo Dubai, in 2020, was an important moment for Delta’s presence in the region. It was a multicultural venue, with people from 190 nationalities and an important hub connecting Asia, Europe, and Africa. “We were in the Portugal Pavilion with Chakall, who had a restaurant there.”

In Saudi Arabia, it was with Delta Q that the business took off. “When we finish this conversation, I will have a meeting with our distributor about a large hotel chain in Saudi Arabia that Delta Q is about to enter,” he reveals. It is also a reminder that consumption in hotel rooms is another way to present Portuguese coffee to customers from all over the world.

Portuguese communities abroad were the starting point for the international expansion of Delta – but they have by no means been the end point. “We are not an exporter,” stresses Rui Miguel Nabeiro. “We invest in markets and we want to build our brand, because that is the best contract we can make with any customer: the brand, what it is worth, its attributes, and the quality of its products.” Once the emigrant communities were won over, in recent years the challenge has been to bring the nationals of those countries to the counter as well, and have them say: “I want a Delta.”

“We are brand makers in the geographies where we choose to be present,” adds Alberto Pinto. “In some geographies with greater ambition, with direct operations, and in others with ambition that matches our partners.” The partner is not always a company that supplies cafés, restaurants, and hotels in its country, or a retailer with shops across the territory. Sometimes the partner can simply be a man who fell in love with Delta. In South Korea, that man is called Ki Seok Lee.

The first two weeks caused concern. But in the third week, customers began to try it and did not stop. In January 2021, the second café opened, strategically close to the Portuguese and Brazilian embassies. The combination of Delta coffee and pastel de nata seems to have won over Koreans: the chain is expanding and there are plans to reach 20 stores by the end of 2023.

Managed from the Shanghai delegation, in China, by João Carvalho, South Korea is growing at its own pace. “It is going well, things are moving forward.” The spirit is always the same: be present and grow from there. Rui Miguel Nabeiro concludes: “It is a small business, they are stores, but it is one more market where we have planted our flag.”

# The most special coffee bean

## Details

- **What:** Deltinha
- **Decade:** 1970
- **Where is it:** Across the country

It has been bigger and smaller, rounder and slimmer, darker and lighter. It has been a soft toy, a figurine, and it has even existed in human form, when the full costume was used at events and hugged hundreds of people in a single day. In many shapes and sizes, Deltinha is part of the history of Delta and of the imagination of many Portuguese people, who have been meeting it again over the last five decades, in many different settings.

The small and friendly coffee bean was born in the 1970s as a way to establish Delta in the market. “I always dreamed of Deltinha,” said Rui Nabeiro. “It is one of my masterpieces.” When Delta was founded in 1961, the coffee sector seemed established and hard to enter. The solution was to try different approaches: invest in packaging and door-to-door distribution, make credit easier for customers and – even before calling it marketing – build a close relationship with the public. “At the time, little was done in that area, but I was already dreaming and making it real. Deltinha was a weapon.”

Together with the purchase of coffee, Deltinhas began to be offered from the north to the south of the country. Children adopted them as toys, and they were also displayed in cafés and pastry shops. # “If there were no coffee, I would be nobody.”

Twelve women, united by courage and by the memory of a legacy, created Café de Amboim – under the Impossible Coffees brand.

In the Café de Amboim lot enters the story of how Rui Nabeiro set out for Angola in 1975, in the opposite direction of the Portuguese who were returning. It includes the leading role of the Grupo Nabeiro in the late 1990s and the turn of the century, in the recovery of the coffee industry in Angola, devastated after decades of civil war. And it includes the Impossible Coffees project, dedicated to launching limited editions of rare and sustainable coffees in partnership with local producers and institutions. But above all, it includes the story of the 12 Angolan women who joined forces to keep coffee production alive in the province of Amboim.

“This coffee is a tribute to the strength and determination of the women of the Associação de Mulheres Empreendedoras do Amboim,” said Rui Miguel Nabeiro, at the launch of this special lot from the Cuanza-Sul region: Café de Amboim. The new edition of Impossible Coffees reaches the market after series dedicated to coffee from the Azores archipelago and from the island of São Tomé. This coffee, said the CEO of Grupo Nabeiro, “is the result of the courage of 12 women who turned adversity into opportunity, keeping production in the region alive and preserving a coffee that is unique in the world.”

## Robust tradition

For Delta, Angola was already more than just one of the many international markets where the company is present. “It is an extension of our identity,” he stressed. In 1975, the country was the fourth largest coffee producer in the world, with an annual output of 200,000 tonnes. It was even the largest source of green coffee for Delta. It is no coincidence, either, that the consumption of robusta coffee has a long tradition in Portugal, to the detriment of arabica varieties. These are acquired tastes and, once rooted, they remain.

Aware of how the national market depended on Angolan production and foreseeing major political changes in the country, Rui Nabeiro went to Angola in 1975, when most Portuguese people were travelling in the opposite direction. He secured something essential for the future of Delta Cafés: he ensured tens of thousands of sacks of coffee. In the aftermath of Angola’s independence, Delta had its warehouses full.

In the late 1990s, the Angolan government approached Delta Cafés about the possibility of revitalising a production unit. This led to the rehabilitation and modernisation of a factory that had been inactive since 1984 and to the creation of Angonabeiro, a Grupo Nabeiro company that operates in Angola.

As for the Impossible Coffees, they are much more than coffee. They are a unique project in entrepreneurship and social activism – driven by Clara Melícias, B2C director at Grupo Nabeiro, created exclusively for [Delta The Coffee House Experience](https://deltacoffeehouse.com/en/) – that shares the stories of people who have always believed in themselves and in their dreams. The result is a collection of rare coffees, sourced from micro-productions in several regions of the world, such as the editions dedicated to the Azores (Café dos Açores) and São Tomé (Café Catoninho).

## The courageous coffee of 12 women

The third edition of Impossible Coffees is dedicated to Amboim. “It is a very specific coffee from Angola, from the Cuanza Sul region,” says Joana Miranda, marketing director at Angonabeiro, who followed this project locally. The project is also a celebration of stories of perseverance and resilience. “It was produced by 12 women who joined forces and formed the Associação de Mulheres Empreendedoras do Amboim to keep coffee production alive in this region, because, with the war, coffee production was forgotten, as were other forms of production that used to exist here.”

This is, then, a story shaped by courage, willpower, and great resilience, led by women who fight every day against adversity and who came together at a time when the promotion of culture was under threat from the effects of the colonial war, the lack of financial resources, and the shortage of labour. “Many are widows and live in very precarious conditions,” says the marketeer. “But with the support of Delta, and also of the Instituto Nacional do Café de Angola, they managed to turn their ambition into a unique women-led entrepreneurship project, through which they support their community by producing coffee. It is the coffee of courage of Angolan women – that is how we define it.”

Lucinda Cunha is one of these women. A coffee producer, she is also responsible for the group of women entrepreneurs in Amboim. “Our connection to coffee goes back a long way, already from the time of our grandparents. We inherited this legacy from our parents, and we do not want to lose this identity – also because coffee has already built cities and has meant a lot to us. We do not want to lose that,” she stresses. “When a person has shed blood on a piece of land, they do not want to give it up for nothing.”

This feeling of resilience, of not giving up – “because they still carry within them the pain of the war” – became clear to Gildo Mariano, CEO and founder of Team Films, the Angolan production company responsible for the photographs and promotional films for this Impossible Coffee, when he visited some of these women on their farms in Amboim. The municipality, in the province of Cuanza Sul in Angola, with its seat in the city of Gabela, is a historic coffee-growing region, with families who have devoted themselves to this crop for several generations. It is also a region where, as Gildo discovered, time is in fact very relative: “They would say that the next farm was 5 minutes away, but then it was almost an hour!”

Gildo explains that the fact many of these women no longer have their husbands – “because many lost their lives in the war we had in Angola” – is an extra reason for them not to give up and to keep working the land as best they can, with all the risks involved.

What impressed him most was the fearlessness with which those women led the work on the farms. “We are talking about men who are former military, but who listened to and respected the women producers.” Gildo remembers a woman telling him that she had taken the reins of the farm since her husband’s death. She told him: “Here I play the man’s role. I walk with my stick, which is a cane, but at the right moment it becomes a whip.” And he concludes: “They are strong women, resilient, determined.”

## The new impossible lot

“That is why we remain in coffee production,” says Lucinda Cunha, stressing that in Angola it is not only men who work with coffee. “We have young women, older women. We are all connected to coffee. It is already in our blood.”

The Café de Amboim in the Impossible Coffees edition is being sold in Portugal by Delta Cafés. And how does it perform in the cup? When it was placed on a tasting table, Adelino Cardoso, coordinator of the Campo Maior roastery, reacted by praising its flavour, density, and creaminess, “with unique aromatic notes, neutral yet present and striking, together with notes of bitter cocoa and nuts.” “What an excellent coffee!”, he remarked.

With each sale, 20% of the amount goes to the Associação de Mulheres Empreendedoras do Amboim. At the beginning of summer, the funds raised had already exceeded 10,000 euros, an amount that will make it possible to increase support for revitalising the coffee value chain in the region. In addition to financial support – used to buy machetes, hire labour, or even purchase land – there is another very important form of support: training and knowledge sharing. “They learn, on their own land, cultivation techniques and how to identify when the coffee is at the right point to be harvested,” explains Joana Miranda. “Naturally, some already produce and deliver green coffee to us, but others are still starting out. Therefore, this is not a project with a time frame of one or two years; it will have to be longer, because if we plant a coffee plant now, it will only start producing fully in five years’ time.”

In short, just as the plant needs time to grow before it yields the green coffee bean, the support protocol for sustainable development in the region will also need time before it bears fruit. Rui Miguel Nabeiro said: “More and more, we are proving that, in fact, nothing is impossible for us. This project, in particular, is truly inspiring. It is a project of 12 women who had to build their own path in life, as we often say. And they decided to make coffee their way of life – so it has everything to do with us.”
“If there were no coffee, I would be nobody.”
