# Catarina Barreiros

> Happiness will not be found in a shopping mall.

Can our individual choices really have the power to transform the world? In a society of consumption and waste, some people choose a different path, more conscious and responsible. With more than 110,000 followers on social media, Catarina Barreiros turns concerns into actions and problems into solutions, inspiring us to rethink habits and make more sustainable choices through the Do Zero project, which grew from a single Instagram page into a website, a podcast, an ecological store, and even an event that attracted 30,000 people. Accessible and engaging, sharp but never arrogant and always with a smile, Catarina welcomed Rita Nabeiro into her home for an open conversation that reinforces how small gestures can have a huge impact on the planet.

## Environmental Awareness and Early Influences

### You trained in architecture and hold a master’s degree in management. You worked in fashion and digital marketing, but it was in sustainability that you discovered your mission: helping people and companies adopt more ecological and intelligent practices. What first awakened your environmental awareness?

It is very hard to answer, because we always look back, trying to understand which things shaped us, but I am still too close to the starting point to see exactly what. Many factors played a role. First of all, my family. I am the daughter of two teachers. I have a brother with cerebral palsy, and my parents always made us believe that we must stand up for people who face more challenges in life than we do. “The world does not owe you anything; with your privilege, you must do something,” they told us.

Then I had a grandmother in Fundão, who always kept her vegetable garden. She washed the plastic shopping bags and hung them out to dry. At that time, you did not pay for them. She said they had not cost her money, but they had cost someone something. My grandmother always made full use of food. She lived a simpler life and, with only primary school, she was still one of the most intelligent women I knew. I always felt very close to that way of being. Then life unfolded.

### You were a Girl Scout.

What made me really enjoy the outdoors, nature, and the philosophy of leaving the world better than we found it, shaped my principles. Along the way, I met people who inspired me. My husband, for example, was very curious about injustices and made me think. It was very interesting when we met, because he really made me reflect.

Later, I had a high-risk pregnancy. Being a mother, in itself, already leads us to think about what future we want to leave to our children. But with a high-risk pregnancy, I had a great deal of time to think about it. So I began to want to find out more and read everything I could.

## Art, Music, and Burnout

### And here, in this room, I see a harp and a piano, as well as shelves full of books. Does this diversity of interests enrich the way you think?

I think everything we do shapes us, for better and for worse. It is funny because my architecture thesis was about social housing, and in management I wrote a thesis on luxury consumption. They are very different worlds. I have always liked to get to know realities that are diametrically opposed.

Music, art, and reading have always been my escapes. In some way, I found in art the balance for the confusion in my brain. I do many things, not all of them well. I am always unsure about the world and I need the space that music gives me.

A few years ago, I had a burnout. I was in a very bad state and the psychologist asked me what I used to do as a little girl when I wanted to be happy – I would go to the piano. That was what saved me. As I was self-employed, it was not as if I could stop.

### How old were you?

I had burnout three years ago, when I was 29. When my daughter, who started playing the piano this year, sometimes says she does not want to practise, I tell her that music, in this house, is like Portuguese or mathematics: it is something you do. Some subjects teach you logical thinking, others teach you to speak properly and to know your culture, but music is an escape for when the world is in a bad place. I tell her that one day she will understand. And I thank my parents every day for enrolling me in music.

## From Consumerism to Sustainability

### You worked in fashion and digital marketing, and I heard in an interview that you were a bit of a consumerist…

It was not just a little. It was a lot.

### How do you go from one extreme to the other?

I believe we need to know ourselves very well to understand what to do with our lives. I did, in fact, work in luxury fashion, but not with luxury salaries. And because I started working very early, at 18 I was living with my parents but I was already earning money. And what did I spend it on? Clothes.

At a certain point, my husband told me he did not understand. That I was a person so concerned about injustice and then I bought fast fashion produced by child slaves on the other side of the world. In fact, I was not being very consistent. At the time, the [Do Zero](https://dozero.pt/) project was not yet up and running, but I think that was the first click.

This does not mean we need to be extremists. It is possible to find balance. But I know myself. I know I had to be all or nothing. It had to be a radical change. And the truth is that, six years later, it no longer costs me anything at all. But at the time it was a difficult decision.

## Activism and Social Media

### Your words and your attitude are very consistent. Do you feel you are an activist in the full sense of the word?

Yes and no. On the one hand, yes, because I do vocal work for a better future. I draw attention to issues that are sometimes even painful. On the other hand, you will not find me out on the street at a demonstration. I hate crowds of people. It is not my space, I cannot shout louder. I prefer dialogue, although demonstrations are also necessary.

Even though I work with social media, I do not enjoy having too much exposure and having my life completely laid bare. So I try not to shout too much.

### When I interviewed Bumba na Fofinha, she said that once someone told her, about a post with 100,000 likes, that it was almost like filling two Estádio da Luz. That is also the number of people who follow you. You have a voice that reaches many people who like you, but since you deal with polarising topics, I ask: do you also receive opposite reactions?

É impossível estar nas redes sociais sem ter exposição a comentários menos simpáticos. Lido com isso melhor ou pior consoante a minha filha me deixar dormir de noite. Há dias em que só me apetece desistir.

Ainda há pouco tempo tive um vídeo que se tornou viral, que é o pior que me podem fazer. Sim, é giro porque a mensagem chega a muita gente, mas vêm muitas pessoas que não nos conhecem e que têm esse vídeo como primeira impressão. Mas não fazem, na verdade, ideia de quem sou, ao contrário da maioria das mais de 100 mil pessoas que me seguem, que já viram vários vídeos meus, que se identificam comigo e, por isso, se mantêm na comunidade. Ou então não se identificam e não ficam, e está certo, porque não temos todos de gostar do mesmo.

E se a seguir fizer um post que vai contra o que pensam de mim, vão dizer que defraudei as suas expectativas. Isso é um pouco difícil de gerir.

### Do you have stories of people who changed their lives that you can share?

I was told that a girl was thinking of studying management, but decided to go into environmental engineering instead. In other words, she decided her life based on what she saw in my videos. It is a big responsibility.

I also know of a family who went to live in the countryside. They told me that after seeing me so many times talking about Fundão and Alentejo and about living in a calmer way, they dropped everything and went. And many people started living without a car, which is very difficult in Portuguese culture.

## Living Without a Car

### Do you live without a car?

Yes, because I live in Lisbon. In Alentejo it would not work. There is a lack of connectivity between cities, though not so much in Greater Lisbon. In areas with access to the Metro, it is very simple to live without a car.

I take my daughter to school by bicycle. It takes eight minutes. By bus or metro it takes me 20 minutes at most. On foot, it would be 45, so it is not that close.

The other day, we went to a show by bus. Afterwards we wanted to go for lunch in a part of the city where parking is difficult. If we had gone by car, we probably would not have gone to that restaurant. Not having a car gives us freedom. It is a conceptual change. And if we need one, we borrow a car from my father or my parents-in-law. It is not that I never set foot in a car.

## The Do Zero Project

### Returning to the Do Zero project, what began as an Instagram page is now a complete ecosystem. How did all this happen?

Somewhat by chance. While I was at home on sick leave and had plenty of time to read scientific articles on sustainability, I started to show what I was doing to my friends through social media.

### Do you remember your first post?

Exactly. I had done my first bulk shopping and made a post saying that I was going to change my life, that I was going to start living in a calmer and more sustainable way. That day was marked forever, because after publishing the post I found out that my best childhood friend had died. Sustainability helped me in a difficult moment. It gave me something to hold on to.

## Starting a More Sustainable Life

### What do you say to people who feel that being sustainable is difficult or expensive? What advice would you give to someone who wants to start, but does not know how?

It depends on the person’s situation. While it is true that some products are more expensive, it is also true that, overall, you save a lot of money. By not having a car, you save. But if, for a family, that is not viable – for example, for my parents, who have my brother in a wheelchair – we need to understand our own dynamics and what works for us.

The idea is not to have a sustainable lifestyle that creates discomfort and takes away our joy of living; it is to feel well and to realise that there are simple things we can do, such as starting to include one plant-based meal per week, or using a solid shampoo instead of a liquid one.

With small achievements we begin to feel that we can do something, that we have a voice. This does not mean we have to do everything. I do not do everything. There are things I should do, but they do not fit into my life. It is important not to judge others or ourselves, because we are part of a complex system. We are one cog in the mechanism, but we are not the only one. We need change that happens gradually.

### And what simple advice would you give people to start putting into practice in their lives which, if everyone followed, would have a huge impact on the planet?

I usually share tips that deliver maximum impact with minimum effort. The first advice I give to anyone who wants to do something that is easy, that protects the environment and also saves money, is to look at food waste.

For example, over the course of a week, weigh all the food that is thrown away, from peels to leftovers. And try to reduce that waste from week to week. Food waste is one of the main – and controllable – causes of greenhouse gas emissions, due to pesticides, the transport of goods, the refrigeration of food, and the processing it undergoes. All of this generates waste.

### What is the second piece of advice?

The second point is to follow a plant-based diet. Saying this can sometimes be alarming, but no one is saying we all have to be vegan to save the planet. That is not the issue.

It is a diet in line with the traditional Mediterranean pattern, where the plate is mainly made up of plant-based foods. This includes vegetables, oilseeds [nuts], and carbohydrates. All of these should be predominant on the plate, not only for environmental reasons, but also for health. Whenever we try to eat in step with the seasons and with what the land provides, we are also doing something good for ourselves.

## Climate Leadership and the Future

### When you see people with responsibilities setting the wrong example, political leaders questioning science, how does that make you feel?

The first reaction is despair. What am I doing here when the leader of the world’s largest power questions whether greenhouse gases are really that harmful? It is a historic step backwards and it is very draining.

I try to draw inspiration from people who have been doing this for decades and have not given up, such as Professor Júlia Seixas and researcher João Pedro Gouveia. So who am I to be tired after six years working on this?

We must not lose our course: we want to continue to exist as a civilization. The continuity of the planet is not at stake; what is at stake is our own continuity. How do we want to live: with masks and in bunkers or walking in nature, picking wild fruit and dipping our feet in a stream?

## Companies, Greenwashing, and Sustainability

### Do you think companies are already committed to change or are they still more focused on “greenwashing” and creating an appearance of sustainability?

It depends greatly on who is leading the companies. Today, it is easy to send out messages that mean nothing, especially to a less informed public. But as people become better informed, that becomes harder. And it is not in the companies’ interest to be caught off guard. There is much more care about what is said today than five years ago.

And I believe companies have a truly transformative role in society. When a large company changes something, it changes it on a much larger scale than a small one. It is always more beneficial to think about what can be done rather than what is not being done. It is already becoming clear that it is necessary to ensure that companies are transparent about the process.

### The word “sustainable” is one of those buzzwords that covers many different meanings. Do you feel that, from being used so often, it is starting to lose its importance? For you, what does it mean “to be sustainable”?

It has its meaning. It is everything we manage to do that can hold up. But, when it comes to marketing, it leaves room for interpretation. I prefer to think in terms of “more sustainable than”. Because one thing, on its own, is not sustainable. It always depends on several factors.

Let us look at bamboo toothbrushes. They are sustainable, but for whom? My house has mould. If I had a bamboo toothbrush, I would have to replace it every three days. Would that be more sustainable? The bamboo comes from China, where forest policies in terms of environmental certifications are still not spectacular, and then it has to come from the other side of the world. Is it really the best option for me?

## Profit, Purpose, and Entrepreneurship

### As an entrepreneur, has it been difficult for you to find a balance between communicating sustainability and the need for Do Zero, as a company, to generate profit? Does it cause you any crises of conscience?

Constantly. João, who is my husband and our in-house finance person, is always saying, “Catarina, the house has to be paid for.” He is right. We can pay people who work with us fairly and respect our suppliers, but at the end of the day I need to have a salary, otherwise I cannot live. No matter how much goodwill I have, if I have to find another job on the side, I will no longer have time to continue doing what I do. That was a hard realisation for me.

But Do Zero was never a project to make a profit, unlike [Norm](https://dozero.pt/). What I believe, as an entrepreneur, is that we must have profit, but not in everything we do. This has been a learning process, and it helps me feel that life will find its order, that if one day we have less, we have less; that if everything goes wrong, we move to a smaller home.

Professionally, I am ambitious. But I am not greedy. An extra 500 or 1000 euros will not make me happy. What makes me happy is having time to go to Fundão or to welcome friends for dinner at home.

## Norm

### You were talking about Norm, your new project.

It is an underwear brand for menstruation or for light urinary leakage that I started with two partners in November 2023. It is a reusable product that is very useful for most women. It has been interesting because, in addition to having partners, we are managing factories.

And we do not take profits; instead, we reinvest in the company. We have also realised that if the company does not make a profit, it cannot innovate. That was a very recent lesson. If we did not have enough margin on what we sell, we would not be able to move forward with the new product we are about to launch: swimsuits and bikinis with the same purpose.

Companies that do not have the financial reserves to withstand the product development period before launch will struggle to survive in the market over the long term.

## A Cidade do Zero

### Do Zero is a project that you share with your husband, João Barreiros, with whom you also created “a cidade do zero”, an event that has grown from year to year. What does it consist of, exactly?

It was a project that came after the pandemic, in which we wanted to create an ecosystem where people could learn about sustainability. A supermarket with only responsible brands does not exist. Most people do not have access to scientists, researchers, and political figures, but I do. So we wanted to create an immersive experience of what it would be like to live in a more sustainable city.

This implies free access to education, to transport, and that the brands around us commit to circular economy. Everything had to be designed so that we could live an experience of what could be, which is not yet, but which, at the same time, was already happening in Portugal, because the scientists we brought were Portuguese.

In the first edition we had 50 talks and activities. We showed things as practical as repairing shoes or making soap. Practical and theoretical activities so that people could feel empowered for sustainability.

### It was a success.

Yes, and the project grew. The first edition was at Pavilhão do Conhecimento. The second, at Centro Cultural de Belém. The third, at Instituto Superior de Agronomia, where Grupo Nabeiro was strongly present, with Delta, Adega Mayor and Why Not.

And we managed to bring thousands of people to a place where cars were not allowed. Because sustainability is not about what we cannot do. It is about the opportunities that open up when we think about what we want from life. A life in community, oriented towards happiness – and happiness will not be tucked away in a shopping centre on a Saturday afternoon. Happiness is what we can share in common.

## Sustainability as an Opportunity

### This theme creates room for innovation, but perhaps some companies see it as a problem. What do you have to say about these challenges that can be seen as obstacles?

That is exactly the point. I believe these can be opportunities. It is very difficult for sustainability not to pay off for a company. When we talk about saving resources, we talk about saving money. That alone is already a benefit.

Companies that see challenges as opportunities for innovation and development are prepared not only for sustainability but for any challenge that follows. They are resilient. Flexible.

## Energy, Railways, and Public Policy

### You are part of the think tank O Futuro Já Começou, which meets regularly with the President of the Republic. If you were prime minister, what would be your first measures?

I have no intention of going into politics, but I have already put together an electoral programme for a shadow list for the last European elections, and I had the opportunity to sit next to specialists and debate what I would do.

About O Futuro Já Começou, I cannot say much, but I can say that I have brought the decentralisation of energy production to the reflection group many times. Portugal is the second country in Europe with the greatest capacity for decentralised solar energy production. This means we can produce it on rooftops, in car parks. There is no need to clear thousands of cork oaks to build a solar park.

To give a sense of how viable this would be, 50% of the energy in Portugal could come from there. Then we still have centralised solar energy, offshore wind, onshore wind… We can very clearly make our country an example in the use of renewable energy.

Another crucial topic is the development of the railway. It is unbelievable that we do not have a connection to the European capitals. We do not even have it between Lisbon and all the district capitals. It is a nameless stupidity, because from the moment I solve the railway, I can even mitigate the housing crisis.

In the last 20 years we have seen railway stations shut down, when we should have done the opposite. João and I have just taken a 10-day trip through Europe in which we did everything by train, except entering and leaving Portugal.

## Family, Work, and Motherhood

### How do you manage your schedule, with so many projects and motherhood?

I am very fortunate because I live in a 21st-century relationship. João and I are parents in equal measure. Sometimes he is more present, other times I am, but there is one very deliberate choice in our life: family is the priority. Everything else comes after.

If Graça needs us, whatever I have to do that day, including meetings with the President of the Republic, will not happen. I know this is an enormous privilege. I do not accept working at the weekend.

My father has always been self-employed, he is a lawyer, and I feel that he regrets the time he did not spend with us. I see the dedication he has for his grandchildren. I have never asked him about this, because I do not want to hurt him, but if I asked him what his greatest regret is, he would probably say it was not seeing us for weeks on end because he was working.

We are also fortunate to have a large support network, with very available grandparents and friends who are family.

## The Future of Norm and Do Zero

### And how do you imagine your future? What impact would you like these projects to have?

I would like to internationalise Norm so that, in a few years, it is a well-established brand. Also because we produce in Portugal and we see the factory facing greater and greater difficulties, as almost all production moves outside Europe because it is cheaper. And it is an outstanding factory, with a nursery for employees’ children. I would like to see it grow with us. To generate profit, yes, but done properly.

As for Do Zero, I hope it will no longer be necessary to keep talking about these issues. I hope that in a few years I can look back and think: ‘Wow, remember when I had to explain to people the environmental impact of using cleaning cloths instead of kitchen paper?’

### Oh toilet paper!

Now they really are going to say I’m crazy. (laughter)

### I was going to ask you that anyway. (laughter)

Basically, toilet paper uses a huge amount of water to produce. It takes 140 litres per roll. In Portugal, per person, according to PORDATA, we use 2.3 to 2.4 rolls per week. That means around 300 litres of water.

Using a bidet, which is more hygienic, uses much less water. Of course, I always keep paper at home for guests. When people tell me it is disgusting that I do not use toilet paper at home, I answer that I do not shower in paper: I shower in water.

## Greatest Dream

### To conclude, what is your greatest dream?

When I think about where I want to be 20 years from now, I want to be in silence, sitting on the porch of my country house, a small house so it is not hard to clean. I want to have a book on the bedside table, a glass of wine, and I want to simply listen to the birds and watch my chickens run from one side to the other.

I want my dog at my feet and my husband by my side reading a book, and if I feel like it, I get up, go to the room to paint or play the piano and, suddenly, children come in and they are my grandchildren and we prepare a big family lunch.

That is my life dream. To have a peaceful, happy, and calm life.

Can our individual choices really have the power to transform the world? In a society of consumption and waste, some people choose a different path, more conscious and responsible. With more than 110,000 followers on social media, Catarina Barreiros turns concerns into actions and problems into solutions, inspiring us to rethink habits and make more sustainable choices through the Do Zero project, which grew from a single Instagram page into a website, a podcast, an ecological store, and even an event that attracted 30,000 people. Accessible and engaging, sharp but never arrogant and always with a smile, Catarina welcomed Rita Nabeiro into her home for an open conversation that reinforces how small gestures can have a huge impact on the planet.

You trained in architecture and hold a master’s degree in management. Then I had a grandmother in Fundão, who always kept her vegetable garden. She washed the plastic shopping bags and hung them out to dry. At that time, you did not pay for them. And here, in this room, I see a harp and a piano, as well as shelves full of books. Does this diversity of interests enrich the way you think?

I think everything we do shapes us, for better and for worse. It is funny because my architecture thesis was about social housing, and in management I wrote a thesis on luxury consumption. produced by child slaves on the other side of the world. In fact, I was not being very consistent. So I try not to shout too much.

Do you have stories of people who changed their lives that you can share?

I was told that a girl was thinking of studying management, but decided to go into environmental engineering instead. In other words, she decided her life based on what she saw in my videos. Do you live without a car?

Yes, because I live in Lisbon. In Alentejo it would not work. There is a lack of connectivity between cities, though not so much in Greater Lisbon. If we had gone by car, we probably would not have gone to that restaurant. Not having a car gives us freedom. It is a conceptual change. Returning to the Do Zero project, what began as an Instagram page is now a complete ecosystem. How did all this happen?
Somewhat by chance. While I was at home on sick leave and had plenty of time to read scientific articles on sustainability, I started to show what I was doing to my friends through social media.
Do you remember your first post?

Exactly. I had done my first bulk shopping and made a post saying that I was going to change my life, that I was going to start living in a calmer and more sustainable way. That day was marked forever, because after publishing the
I found out that my best childhood friend had died. Sustainability helped me in a difficult moment. It gave me something to hold on to.
What do you say to people who feel that being sustainable is difficult or expensive? What advice would you give to someone who wants to start, but does not know how?

It depends on the person’s situation. While it is true that some products are more expensive, it is also true that, overall, you save a lot of money. By not having a car, you save. But if, for a family, that is not viable – for example, for my parents, who have my brother in a wheelchair – we need to understand our own dynamics and what works for us. The idea is not to have a sustainable lifestyle that creates discomfort and takes away our joy of living; it is to feel well and to realise that there are simple things we can do, such as starting to include one plant-based meal per week, or using a solid shampoo instead of a liquid one. With small achievements we begin to feel that we can do something, that we have a voice. This does not mean we have to do everything. I do not do everything. There are things I should do, but they do not fit into my life. It is important not to judge others or ourselves, because we are part of a complex system. We are one cog in the mechanism, but we are not the only one. We need change that happens gradually.
And what simple advice would you give people to start putting into practice in their lives which, if everyone followed, would have a huge impact on the planet?

I usually share tips that deliver maximum impact with minimum effort. The first advice I give to anyone who wants to do something that is easy, that protects the environment and also saves money, is to look at food waste. For example, over the course of a week, weigh all the food that is thrown away, from peels to leftovers. And try to reduce that waste from week to week. Food waste is one of the main – and controllable – causes of greenhouse gas emissions, due to pesticides, the transport of goods, the refrigeration of food, and the processing it undergoes. All of this generates waste.
What is the second piece of advice?

The second point is to follow a plant-based diet. Saying this can sometimes be alarming, but no one is saying we all have to be vegan to save the planet. That is not the issue. It is a diet in line with the traditional Mediterranean pattern, where the plate is mainly made up of plant-based foods. This includes vegetables, oilseeds [nuts], and carbohydrates. All of these should be predominant on the plate, not only for environmental reasons, but also for health. Whenever we try to eat in step with the seasons and with what the land provides, we are also doing something good for ourselves.

# 10 years of Centro de Ciência do Café

To mark the 10th anniversary of CCC, we present 10 key works from its collection and the same number of reasons to visit.

## Helena Nabeiro

### At the Centro de Ciência do Café since the first day

The Centro de Ciência do Café was a long-held dream of Rui Nabeiro, fulfilled on the day he turned 83, on 28 March 2014. “I am a dreamer of knowledge. Each person owns their own attitude, and mine is knowledge and sharing it with other people,” he stated at the inauguration of the 3,500-square-metre building designed by architect João Simão.

The glazed façade facing the Adega Mayor vineyard, next to the Delta factory facilities, two minutes from Campo Maior, marks the evolution of the former Museu do Café – expanded, modernised, and transformed – into the Centro de Ciência do Café, exactly 10 years ago. And it took only one more year for it to be recognised by the Associação Portuguesa de Museologia with the Prémio Museu Português, a distinction earned by those who have cared for the Centre from the beginning and by its team: Helena Nabeiro.

The current interpretation and science and technology outreach centre is one of the projects that the administrator of Grupo Nabeiro has embraced with greatest dedication. It was already so before the Centre became a Centre – it was Rui Nabeiro’s daughter who was given the task of inaugurating the former Coffee Museum, in December 1994. For almost 30 years, Ms. Lena – as her friends call her – has been responsible for everything related to the Group’s museum space, its activities, temporary exhibitions, and the curation of the permanent collection.

“Centro de Ciência do Café aims to be a meeting place for people from many different fields and interests,” explains the manager, “offering for this purpose a temporary exhibition space where, side by side with science, we intend to promote the dissemination of art and culture.”

It is a space designed for all visitors, with interaction, multimedia components, and exhibitions that tell the story of coffee and everything around it. At the entrance, the floor shows the footprints of the Mico Estrela, a small rodent that is a frequent visitor to coffee plantations in Brazil and the mascot of the Centro de Ciência do Café. Its footprints mark the route. Let us follow them.

## Fauna and flora

### Like a coffee plantation, but indoors

The Mico Estrela footprints first lead us to the greenhouse area, where the humid climate of a coffee plantation is recreated, with striking coffee trees of the arabica and robusta species. Here, visitors can see something unique in Europe: coffee plants bearing the fruits that will become the green beans to be roasted, ground, extracted, and served in a cup. It is something unique, but only in mainland Portugal, since in the Azores archipelago the climatic conditions now allow Delta to do something once thought impossible: produce coffee at scale.

Beyond the heat and humidity in the air, and the smell of the soil, twice a year the greenhouses gain an added interest: the chance to see coffee trees in bloom in person. It is a phenomenon that lasts only three days, says Cristina Gameiro, museologist and curator of the Centro de Ciência do Café.

The experience is complemented by infographics and supporting texts placed throughout the Centre. In this case, they explain planting systems, pruning, soil conditions, the coffee cherry, the harvest, and what happens next to the coffee beans. “People also come to get to know the plant, the flower, the fruit, and to become aware of that tropical climate.”

With the question of flora resolved, the focus turns to fauna. As visitors leave the greenhouse, passing walls lined with encyclopedic information about coffee culture around the world and the largest producing countries, a smaller room invites a closer look. It is the insectarium room, which reveals the insects found in coffee plantations. “Each one has its role,” explains the museologist. “We have the good insects and the bad ones, those that introduce pests and those that clean the roots of the coffee trees, eat the rotten fruit, and pollinate the plants.” As a point of interest, all the insects on display come from Portuguese-speaking coffee-producing countries, such as Angola, São Tomé, or Timor.

Beyond the heat and humidity in the air, and the smell of the soil, twice a year the greenhouses gain an added interest: the chance to see a coffee plant without blossom in person. It is a phenomenon that lasts only three days.

## The history of coffee…

### From the origins of the drink to its arrival in Portugal

The route offers visitors several sensory experiences, such as stepping into the role of a green coffee bean during roasting by entering a roasting sphere that simulates the process. Before that, however, a short animated film of just seven minutes, *The Legend of Kaldi*, presents the ancient origins of coffee, which emerged in the 14th century in the so-called “Horn of Africa”, most likely in Ethiopia.

We reached the upper floor, the wing dedicated to History, explaining how Portugal, although not a producer, has a long tradition in coffee. The short answer is: it was in the reign of King João V, at the beginning of the 18th century, that the coffee trade began to develop. Here is the long answer: because the king, having learned that the French and the English traded coffee in international markets, unlike the Portuguese, sent Francisco de Mello Palheta to French Guiana with the mission of taking coffee plants to Brazil, where the climate would be favourable for production.

“It is said that Francisco de Mello Palheta arrived in French Guiana, but he could not get the governor to sell him the plants. However, during his stay he formed a strong relationship with the governor’s wife, and it was she who, when she realized he was going to return to Brazil without the plant, offered him a bouquet of flowers – and hidden in it were the little cherries, the fruit that yields the coffee seeds,” says Cristina Gameiro, who holds a degree in History and a postgraduate qualification in Museology. “Even today the Palhete coffee brand is still sold in Brazil.”

An interactive video simulates sea voyages on board a galleon. As they travel from port to port, visitors learn a little history. They learn, for example, what life on board was like. The food that rotted. The importance of the water carrier, the person responsible for rationing and distributing water to the crew. They also learn – or are reminded – that it was not only coffee that came from the colonies to the capital of the empire: in different periods of Portuguese maritime expansion, the ships arrived loaded with gold, diamonds, spices, cocoa, or enslaved people.

An interactive video simulates sea voyages on board a galleon. As they travel from port to port, visitors learn a little history.

## … and coffee in history

### From the most emblematic cafés to smuggling on the border

For Cristina Gameiro, one of the main attractions of the [Centro de Ciência do Café](https://www.centrocienciacafe.com/pt) is the interactivity and modern character of the space and its museography. All the content was designed in a didactic and playful way so that people of all ages can learn while they enjoy themselves. “The space is 10 years old and during this period it has been constantly improved, the software updated, and the heritage preserved in the best possible condition.”

An example of this is the table placed in front of a green screen in the historic cafés area. Visitors are invited to sit down and have their photograph taken with a digital background that virtually transports them to the country’s most emblematic cafés, such as Majestic in Porto, Martinho da Arcada in Lisbon, or Luiz da Rocha in Beja. The photograph is sent automatically to their email or social media. “It serves to remind us that cafés once meant much more than simple places to have a drink,” he says. “Today they are very focused on tourism, but in the past they were meeting points for politicians, intellectuals, artists, students, and businesspeople.”

In another room, still on the upper floor, you can hear the stories of those who devoted their lives to coffee smuggling, an activity that supported entire families in a time of hardship, from the 1930s to the 1960s. “Smuggling along the border was the foundation of economic development not only in Campo Maior, but across the whole region,” the museologist recalls.

Here the analogue merges with the digital. At one end there is a coffee sack with an adapted handle that allowed it to be carried like a backpack, and the belt-sling that could hold one kilo – if the guards appeared, the sack was dropped to speed up the escape, but not the belt. At the other end there is a video game for two players, in which we become smugglers: the goal is to follow a route while escaping the guards, until the players manage to get coffee across the border. The faster they are, the more points they earn.

In another room, still on the upper floor, you can hear the stories of those who devoted their lives to coffee smuggling, an activity that supported entire families in a time of hardship, from the 1930s to the 1960s.

## The former museum

### Art, culture, and the collections on display

“Of all the cafés in the world, you had to walk into mine,” says Humphrey Bogart’s character to Ingrid Bergman’s in *Casablanca*. In *La Dolce Vita*, Federico Fellini shows the lively cafés on the elegant streets of Rome. The actress Jeanne Moreau gives one of her finest performances in *The Lovers of Montparnasse*, which showcases the historic Café Domme, a classic among Parisian cafés. These are only three examples of cafés that have left their mark on the seventh art. An interactive panel on the ground floor shows film scenes – from these and others – in which movie stars share the spotlight with cafés.

After the film session, visitors enter the museum space of the Centro de Ciência do Café, where collections of historical, cultural, and technological objects associated with coffee are on permanent display. It has been this way since the days of the Museu do Café, which operated between 1994 and 2014, the year CCC opened. “We moved from an old museum with 800 m² to this Centre with 3,500 m²,” notes Cristina Gameiro, who began her connection to Grupo Nabeiro precisely in 1994.

The Museum collections – such as old roasters, grinders, sack coffee machines, balloon machines with oil lamps, and other domestic and industrial coffee machines – were moved to the Centre. On display is Delta’s heritage, such as the first earthenware cup from the 1970s, but also many cups from competitors, because, as the museologist explains: “This is not the Delta Science Centre, it is the Coffee Centre.”

Again on the upper floor, but now above the reception and facing the vineyards, there is a space that hosts temporary exhibitions. There is also a small library dedicated to the usual theme, with specialist books and magazines, and a reading room.

The Museum collections – such as those of old roasters, grinders, sack coffee machines, balloon machines with oil lamps, and other domestic and industrial coffee machines – were transferred to the CCC.

## Sensory experience

### The Coffee Science Centre is a place to experience with all your senses.

At the Aroma Table, visitors face a blind test. “It is no different from a wine tasting,” says Cristina. The difference is that nothing is drunk; everything is smelled. Under each tap on the table, there is a mirrored surface and a button. When the button is pressed for the first time, a scent is released. You bring your nose close and try to identify it. Vanilla, mint, hazelnut, jasmine, cinnamon, and lemon are the options. Think you know it? Press a second time and the mirrored surface reveals the answer.

After using your sense of smell, it is time to see with your hands. That is, to fill your hands with coffee beans of the arabica, robusta, and mocca varieties, and to feel the differences. And nearby, continuing to engage the senses, there is a sensory analysis of the coffee, exactly as the Delta technicians carry out in the laboratory to assess the quality of the beans. Visitors are invited to taste 100% arabica coffee and 100% robusta coffee. The spittoon is only used if you wish, but be aware that it is part of the process.

If you do not suffer from claustrophobia, the virtual roasting chamber is an experience not to be missed. It is, in fact, very likely that you will not have another chance to put yourself in the place of a green coffee bean while it is exposed to the extreme temperatures of roasting – unless you return to the Coffee Science Centre. Whether you are coming back or visiting for the first time, children are more than welcome. In fact, Cristina Gameiro notes that at weekends many parents come at their children’s request.

Coffee Kids is to blame: a space dedicated to the youngest visitors, where they can jump into a giant cup-shaped ball pit and draw on the walls with digital pens that leave no ink, but tell the ceiling projector where to cast the “digital paint”. Meanwhile, adults can take the opportunity to learn how to pull the perfect espresso, understand the benefits of coffee, or debunk myths about decaffeinated.

After using your sense of smell, it is time to see with your hands. That is, to fill your hands with coffee beans of the arabica, robusta, and mocca varieties, and to feel the differences.

## Eternally Rui Nabeiro

### The legacy of the Comendador and coffee, always coffee

It is always worth recalling that the Centro de Ciência do Café focuses on a universe that goes beyond the already vast boundaries of Grupo Nabeiro. In other words, this is not Delta’s science centre. Even so, and unsurprisingly, Delta coffee also inspires pilgrimages – in more than one sense.

“Many people arrive and ask about the factory. They want to see the place where the coffee they drink every day comes from,” says Cristina Gameiro. “As the factory cannot be visited, because food processing facilities have restricted access, they come to the CCC to gain an idea of the journey the coffee takes before it reaches the cup.”

There are also those who visit because of Senhor Comendador. “In this year since his passing, the Centre has begun to receive visits from people who never met him in person, and who now want to understand his legacy better,” says Cristina Gameiro. The museologist recalls a recent visit from a retired military couple: “They came here, had lunch at Herdade dos Adaens, visited the Centre and Adega Mayor, and even went to the cemetery to leave a flower.”

Since 28 March, the birthday of Rui Nabeiro, it has been possible to learn more about the legacy of the founder of Delta without leaving the Centro de Ciência do Café. On that day, the first phase of an exhibition dedicated to his life and work, “E/Ternamente Rui Nabeiro”, was inaugurated. The exhibition will expand over the year with new phases and can be visited until 28 March 2025.

Then there are those who return almost every week. They are the loyal admirers of a coffee blend created by Rui Nabeiro, whose arabica and robusta ratio is a secret, and which is sold only here, at the Alquimia do CCC shop. They come back to replenish their coffee stock at home – it is sold in bulk, as whole beans or ground on the spot, just like the other specialty coffees from various origins – and they also take the opportunity to order it in the cup, prepared by baristas with specific training that allows them to extract the coffee in a way that makes full use of its qualities.

Anyone who wants to learn how to pull the perfect espresso is in the right place. In addition to Academia Barista, which trains professionals and enthusiasts who wish to deepen their relationship with coffee, the Alquimia store also offers workshops and tastings. For coffee lovers, there is no other place like this.

# Dómúz, a classic at the service of mixology

According to its general director, Pedro Foles, “it is almost a refounding of the brand.”

“It is a positive evolution. The bottles used to be tall, now they are short, and the labels, and even the logo, are completely different,” sums up André Coelho, from Co&K, the agency that coordinated the rebranding of Dómúz, a national reference in the 60s and 70s thanks to its anise liqueurs—the traditional, transparent one, and “Mel de Damas”, sweeter and aimed at a female audience. Times have changed and, with them, the tastes and preferences of consumers.

“We had to reconsider everything,” says Pedro Foles, general manager of Adega Mayor, who now faces the challenge of managing Dómúz. “It is the group’s oldest brand, founded in 1932, even before Camelo cafés, and we did not want to give it up,” he adds. And he stresses: “A brand that lasts almost one hundred years certainly has value, and a story to tell, which needs to be brought into the present day. That was our starting point.”

This blend has Delta quality, a leader in the coffee bean segment, and it arrives to make a difference in the coffee ritual of the Portuguese.

Of course, if there were still a spectrum of regular Dómúz consumers, such a disruptive rebranding might not be advisable, but that is not the case. “The consumer who lived through that moment of greater visibility, of greater expansion of the brand, today no longer has a relationship with it. It is a brand that means nothing to young people, and that older people, who remember it, have stopped consuming,” says Pedro Foles, recalling that “it was a range that was dormant within Grupo Nabeiro.”

The anise liqueurs will be discontinued, as they do not have the potential to justify their maintenance. This is not the case for the coffee and bitter almond varieties. “Now, in the first year, we aim at least to double the brand’s sales, but we believe that growth may be much more significant than that.”

In fact, depending on how the market responds, Dómúz liqueurs with other aromas may even be created. But without rushing: “The brand is now being reborn with these two references, but the vision is that, further ahead, it will be expanded with other drinks that are relevant for our clients and consumers.”

The Portuguese will not be the only ones to shape its future: “The brand has international distribution, with a particular presence in Spain, where it has taken root, associated with the habit of the chupito, which is the equivalent of our abaladiça, that drink offered after a meal or after coffee.”

In this sense, in the Portuguese market, liqueurs are also mostly taken as digestifs, competing with Port wine and Madeira, among others. But these in particular have a different consumption opportunity: “They are moments of enjoyment outside meals, when liqueurs can be consumed on their own or in cocktails.” Bitter almond is excellent for late afternoons, served simply with ice and lemon. And coffee liqueur is also drunk just with ice and lemon: it is a drink similar to the so-called mazagrin, but with alcohol.

What is certain is that the liqueur category has been growing, and this is mainly due to the development of mixology. “Coffee liqueur, for example, is part of the recipe of one of the most sought-after cocktails today, the Espresso Martini,” adds Pedro Foles, noting that an omnichannel distribution strategy will be followed.

“Bars, cafés and restaurants will be the first channel to explore, followed by the retail channel, in order to offer accessibility that is consistent with the brand’s matrix.” Noting that consumption habits are changing—“there is a group of this type of drinks with greater uptake, and a segment of the population that looks for innovation, that even within what may be a historic brand, looks for novelty”—this rebranding of Dómúz is entirely logical.

## Future with History

“Taking the heritage and reinventing it for the future, for the art of mixology” was, according to André Coelho, the coordinator of this rebranding, the challenge that Adega Mayor set for the agency Co&K. “We were challenged to transform a brand that is almost one hundred years old, and the transformation was enormous,” he states.

It all began in December 2024—and the result is already visible to consumers this summer.

The story goes back to 1932, when three partners from Elvas founded Dómúz—named after the Latin expression *Domus mea est orbis meus*, “my home is my world”. Two of them were pharmacists and, through their profession, they knew the secrets of mixing natural ingredients and creating syrups and elixirs—a kind of alchemy, a word that comes from the Greek for “fusion of liquids”. Using the same principles on which they based their remedies, they created appetising liqueurs—with a syrup base, nothing more than a combination of distilled water and sugar to give sweetness, an aroma (in this case anise, since bitter almond and coffee are more recent flavours) and aguardente.

The brand’s rebranding is a tribute to this connection with the pharmacy, but “it is important that this is clear,” stresses André Coelho, “that Adega Mayor wants to move away from that universe, from that idea of medicines and chemistry, which today is not well regarded; people look for what is more natural and made in an artisanal way.”

The inspiration was therefore “the pharmacy as alchemy, or even a more futuristic concept of mixology, the art of creating and mixing drinks and flavours.” It is, to a certain extent, a return to the roots, but adapted to the present world, in which cocktails are in fashion, as well as the bartenders who create them, late summer afternoon parties, the traditional amêndoa amarga drunk from a modern glass…

The key to the (good) result was that workshop. Several paths were proposed, post-its with ideas spread across the walls, and the rebranding concept was gradually narrowed down: “I even considered blue glass bottles, but the Adega Mayor team immediately showed me that was not the way to go. In one afternoon, we gained a week of work.”

Produced in a glass factory in Marinha Grande, using recycled glass, the new bottles for Dómúz liqueurs are therefore transparent, highlighting the colour of the liqueur itself. As for the shape, they are “inspired by the typical pharmacy bottle, which is completely disruptive compared to the original ones”. In addition, “they are closer to what is considered traditional today, even in the gin segment”.

The labels are also completely different from those that previously identified the brand: “They are inspired by pharmacy labels. They have a white background and then an orange band for the coffee liqueur and a blue band for the bitter almond liqueur.”

The Dómúz team did not bring preconceived ideas to the workshop, but it knew what mattered and needed emphasis: “Dómúz predates Delta and was a remarkable brand, with significant consumption, when Mr. Rui Nabeiro joined it through his commercial strength, which also carried great emotional value. In other words, it was a classic, and that could not be overlooked. On the other hand, with the passing of time, changing tastes, and the arrival in Portugal of a group of multinational brands that drove the evolution, diversification, and sophistication of this beverage category, the brand went into decline.”

With the reorganisation of the group and the governance model that placed Dómúz under the management team of Adega Mayor, it became clear that the brand still had enormous potential. This was the starting point for this rebranding, which is almost a refounding of Dómúz: “It was necessary to reinvent a classic, to modernise everything without giving up its history, and to respond to the trend of mixology, which still has significant room to grow.”

# Café embraced by the Atlantic

The first Portuguese coffee is grown in the Azores and results from a partnership with local producers and regional institutions.

Report on Terceira Island, where what once seemed almost impossible has become reality.

## The History of Coffee in the Azores

The history of coffee in the Azores is not linear. Before reaching the Delta The Coffee House Experience stores in Lisbon and Porto, where it is sold under the name The Impossible Coffee, Azorean coffee overcame barriers and opened new horizons.

The exact moment when it was introduced in the archipelago is unknown, but it is estimated that the origin of coffee cultivation dates back to the late eighteenth century. We know this from references to its cultivation found in literature of the time, such as in the work *Escavações* (1821), in the pamphlet *Ensaio sobre a Cultura Preferível para Substituir os Cereais na Ilha de S. Miguel, e os meios de a Promover* (1840), or in the periodical *O Agricultor Micaelense* (1844).

Coffee growing was seen as a curiosity. It served ornamental purposes more than any commercial logic, but there were exceptions. And those had their centre on Terceira Island, where the 12 sacks of coffee came from that reached São Miguel in the summer of 1848, according to the July edition of *O Agricultor Micaelense*. By comparison, in May 15 sacks had arrived from Pernambuco, in Brazil, then the main coffee exporter to the Azores.

Several plantations appeared on the island in the second half of the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th century, but they have since disappeared. In the 1970s, after 25 de Abril, the Official Agricultural Services launched a campaign to encourage the cultivation of Arabica coffee in the Caturra and Yellow Bourbon varieties, brought from Brazil, which adapted well to this subtropical climate. However, the lack of technical knowledge and of suitable equipment for processing and storage after harvest condemned the campaign to failure.

At the turn of the millennium, several technicians from the Terceira Agricultural Development Service resumed coffee planting, using the island’s most productive “mother plants” as a basis, and then passed them on to farmers and producers interested in the crop.

But first, the technicians carried out an exhaustive survey of the coffee trees on the island. “We can still find some very old specimens on Terceira, approximately 80–90 years old, and some already over a hundred years old. We recorded 213 locations with coffee trees of different types, from new plantations to working farms and abandoned farms, public gardens, private gardens, and so on,” explains Jorge Tiago Martins, one of the technicians who started planting coffee more than 20 years ago.

## Coffee Across the Archipelago

Jorge grew coffee on the island where he lives, Terceira, but the entire archipelago has potential and small-scale production for local consumption or for creating its own brands.

This is the case of Fajã dos Vimes, on the island of São Jorge, where the first coffee plants arrived from Brazil about 200 years ago and where the Nunes families have more than one hectare planted behind their house—these plants descend from those that arrived at the beginning of the 19th century. The annual harvest has given rise to brands aimed mainly at tourists.

From São Miguel comes the example of Pedro Pimentel and Dina Fraga, a couple who always remembered seeing Caturra coffee plants in São Miguel, because the flowers, beautiful, are unforgettable. After deciding to invest in coffee production, they imported seeds, found a nursery grower who taught them how to plant coffee trees and, soon, they will have 9,000 plants producing coffee beans.

The seed took root and, from 2010 onwards, a small group of producers formed Companhia Insulana de Cafés, an organization created to promote coffee cultivation. In 2015, it gave way to [Associação de Produtores Açorianos de Café – APAC](https://apac-cafe-dos-acores.negocio.site/), which today has “70 members on eight of the nine islands,” according to Luis Espínola, who chairs the association.

## The Partnership Behind The Impossible Coffee

In recent years, together with APAC, the regional government and with support from foreign specialists, [Delta Cafés](https://deltacafes.com/) has carried out studies to identify which species would be best suited to the Azorean climate and soil, confirming that there are six Arabica coffee varieties with potential to be produced in the archipelago.

“We have invested in the training and qualification of coffee growers in the Azores, with more than 1,200 hours of field work so far. Over these last years, we have supported more than 80 producers through capacity-building actions and workshop,” says the CEO of Delta Cafés, Rui Miguel Nabeiro. “Thanks to them, coffee production has returned to the archipelago, and many now invest in small-scale coffee production.”

The launch by [Grupo Nabeiro](https://gruponabeiro.com/) of The Impossible Coffee, a 100% Azorean coffee blend, marks a clear statement of the project’s quality.

“Our coffee is moving from being sold in small-producer batches under their own brands to a stage where it can be tasted alongside other coffees of the highest quality,” says Luís Espínola, president of APAC. “The partnership with Delta Cafés, APAC and the Regional Government of the Azores is essential to provide the tools needed for coffee to become more than a dream, a reality.”

## Questions and Answers

### 1. Does presenting a coffee grown in the Azores have any special meaning?

The project itself is inspiring, and the fact that it is in the Azores makes all the difference. There is a set of factors that is hard to explain, but you can feel a deep passion for our ability to produce coffee in Portugal and, in particular, in the Azores, which is the only place in Europe where this is possible. Delta is very proud to present the first Portuguese coffee.

### 2. That is why the café is called Impossible Coffee?

As one of the largest consumers and a place where coffee culture has been established for a long time, Europe did not produce coffee because the climate was not suitable. That is why we called it Impossible Coffee. Because what matters most is making the impossible possible.

### 3. How did Delta become involved in this project?

In 2018, Delta joined International Coffee Partners, an association of European family-owned companies in the coffee business, created to support the development of production among smallholder farmers. At that time, we learned that there was an attempt to grow coffee in the Azores. That was when we thought: ‘Why not?’ Why not try to understand whether it is possible to take this step? We did not expect to be the farmers ourselves. What we wanted, and still want, is to inspire families and small producers to believe that it is possible to invest in coffee and make a living from its cultivation.

### 4. What conditions does this archipelago offer that cannot be found in the rest of Europe?

The Azores have a favourable climate: very humid, with constant rain and mild temperatures. The volcanic soil itself, which we might think could make planting difficult, turns out to have—as we now know, after four years of studies—optimal conditions for producing at least six coffee species. What we will see later is whether we meet this expectation. What we did first was to study in order to gain knowledge. Then we shared this knowledge with the regional government and with APAC [association of producers]. Together, we are transforming the present to create a future for coffee growers in the Azores.

### 5. And how would you describe coffee from the Azores?

It is a specialty coffee, with a very distinctive taste and extremely high quality. Volumes will not be large, but it will be, above all, a very, very good coffee.

## The Coffee Tree Nursery

There are 6,240 plants from six varieties of the Arabica species under the care of the nurseries of the Agriculture Division of the Terceira Agrarian Development Service. From here, coffee trees are sent to the rest of the archipelago. This is where everything happens.

The most recent survey counted 12,000 Arabica coffee plants, of the Caturra and Yellow Bourbon varieties, on Terceira Island. Of these, around 600 were between 10 and 30 years old, and 300 plants were over 30 years old—including some that are over a century old—with production levels considered excellent. As for productive coffee trees, the Terceira Agricultural Development Service estimates there are around 4,500, that is, plants more than three years old—the remaining plants are younger.

So that producers do not waste time and resources on plants that end up not developing or not producing what is expected of them, the Agriculture Division of the Agricultural Development Service of Terceira created a coffee tree nursery. This support structure for coffee production is a kind of daycare where 6,240 “babies”—from six varieties of the Arabica species—are under the care of Jorge Azevedo, the agronomist responsible for the project.

From this nursery on Terceira, between 4,000 and 5,000 coffee plants are sent out every year to be grown on the other islands of the archipelago. They are “mother plants”, the result of genetic improvement carried out by the team led by Jorge Azevedo. They are accompanied by technical advice, collection of soil samples from the plots where they will be planted, as well as guidance on fertility, installation and planning of new plantations, crop management, and post-harvest treatment.

“We are developing six new Arabica varieties and comparing them with the two reference ones,” says Jorge, referring to Caturra and Yellow Bourbon, the two varieties that have dominated the coffee landscape of the Azores since the eighteenth century. The aim is to understand whether they perform well in this climate and terroir. “We observe their agronomic adaptation: resistance to cold, to dryness, whether ripening is uniform, resistance to diseases, and whether they have higher productivity.” If coffee production in the Azores is already going well, expectations for the future are even brighter.

## Jorge Tiago Martins, the Engineer

Jorge Tiago Martins is an agronomist and is part of the technical team of the Serviço de Desenvolvimento Agrário da Terceira, which more than 20 years ago had the idea of restoring coffee cultivation. They decided to do this because it was a crop that already existed on the island, but production was very disorganized. “People grew coffee for their own consumption or kept the plants to decorate their land, because the trees have very striking, very vivid green foliage,” he explains.

“Production is now more organised,” he notes. “Some producers have small brands of their own, and then there are those who produce but are not interested in creating brands,” says Jorge, who belongs to this group. The agronomist starts the harvest at the end of May, beginning of June. All production follows organic farming, with coffee plants growing alongside other fruit trees typical of subtropical climates, such as citrus, avocados, guava and passion fruit.

Part of what he harvests stays on his farm on the outskirts of Angra do Heroísmo—“here in this area you find several farms with century-old coffee plants,” he notes—where it will be served at breakfast over the following months; the rest is sold to another producer on the island who, in this case, has a brand and then markets it—that is the part of the process that does not interest him at all.

“Coffee does not tolerate temperatures below 5 or 6 degrees Celsius, and we do not have that in the islands,” says Jorge. “It is not enough to have hot summers; the minimum temperatures must stay above 10 degrees, and that does not happen on the mainland.” This climate is not exclusive to the Azores, which is why Madeira and the Canary Islands also have coffee plants.

Each mature Arabica coffee tree that Jorge has scattered across the land around his house—mixed with other fruit trees and sheltered from the wind behind hedges—produces between 900 and 1,200 grams of green beans, which are ready for roasting. “That is five times less than the fruit,” he notes, before showing why he has to pick five kilos of coffee cherries to obtain one kilo of green coffee. “After we pick the ripe fruit, we let it dry, we peel it down to the pulp as if it were a cherry, and we take the seed, which is the bean.”

Jorge believes that better organization is also visible in technical support during cultivation and post-harvest. “It is essential,” he states. “It is a process that can ruin a good coffee. The coffee can be good, from good plants and with good yields, but poor handling after harvest—from drying to pulping, from roasting to storage—can spoil all the coffee.” This means, in the view of this agronomist, that “around 80% of the conditions needed to produce a good coffee are linked to post-harvest.”

With good storage conditions, green coffee keeps for up to one year. “In a good warehouse, with controlled temperature and humidity, and no sources of contamination, coffee can keep for a very long time.” Once it is roasted, it must then be sold as quickly as possible so it does not lose its freshness. “It is different from the fresh fruit business,” he says—and, in case there was any doubt, yes, coffee is a fruit and its plant, the coffee tree, is a fruit tree.

## José Gabriel Ferreira, the American

The café began 12 years ago as a pastime for this former emigrant to the United States. “A hobby,” as José Gabriel Ferreira explains, in immaculate American-accented speech. “One day when I went to São Jorge, a friend of mine who had coffee trees that were 70 and 80 years old asked me why I did not take coffee back to Terceira.” José Gabriel replied that he knew little about the subject, and his friend answered that he would teach him.

When he returned home, he planted the trees. Some took root, others did not. “If I knew then what I know now, I would have planted more and today I would have a larger yield. This year I only produced 80 kilos, which is little. It is not enough to be able to sell outside,” he laments.

“I have 10 alqueires of land [about one and a half hectares]. I am using six for coffee and I have 1,500 trees planted.” The youngest are two years old. By his calculations, when all of them are producing, he will have around one and a half tonnes to harvest each year. “Then I will already have a strong level of production.”

The plantation is in São Bento, in the southern part of Terceira, a little above Angra do Heroísmo, which from the property looks splendid, with the sea in the background. “I am inside the city and, at the same time, I am outside it. There is no Azores coffee with a better view than this.”

In the first year, the coffee tree produces little. Only after three years does it begin to work at cruising speed. A further three years of experience are added to check the quality of this work, as well as the quantity that results from it. “If a tree does not produce at least 15 kilos, it is no longer a good tree. Because it works at a ratio of five to one,” says 63-year-old José Gabriel Ferreira. “You pick five kilos of fruit to get one kilo of coffee. And after roasting it loses another 20%. Imagine: you pick 15 kilos of coffee fruit and you end up with 2.4 kilos of clean coffee. You need a big tree.”

Like so many Azoreans before him, José emigrated to the United States. He went to the city of San José, in California, at the age of 20, in 1980, to build bathrooms, and returned to the island 18 years later. “I put in my retirement time and came back to my homeland. Today, this plot already gives me enough work to keep me busy all day.”

He works in agriculture full time and, two years ago, he began selling roasted coffee to tourists. He roasts the coffee in a micro-roastery at APAC’s headquarters, with a capacity of one kilo. Before, he produced only for his own consumption. In truth, with a total production of 80 kilos last year, there is not much to sell. This situation will change soon and, José Gabriel Ferreira hopes, with the help of Delta. “Why? Because, in the future, Delta will be good for the Azores. When we are producing 10 or 15 tonnes, who are we going to sell to?”

José never speaks of just one island. He always refers to the group of all nine, to the archipelago. “In the Azores, we are now starting to produce six new coffee varieties. We are trying to understand which one is best for the islands. We know that Yellow Bourbon and Caturra do well here.”

The worst enemy of coffee is the wind. For this reason, José—like the other coffee producers—plants tall hedges to break the wind and protect the coffee trees. “Many trees do not grow any further because of the gusts of wind. The tree we like is low, but has wide branches. Those are the good ones. They will never grow very tall, but they will be good production trees.” When the plant reaches the height of an average man, José tops it so that it starts to grow sideways and not upwards.
